Hon. W. B. NANTEL (Minister of Inland Revenue) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 99, to amend the Adulteration Act. He said:	This Bill provides for several
amendments to the law, but there is only one of very material importance. The following new section is introduced:
No person shall manufacture for sale, keep for sale, or offer or expose for sale, as maple sugar any sugar which is not pure maple sugar, nor as maple syrup any syrup which is not pure maple syrup, and any maple sugar or maple syrup which is not up to the standard prescribed by the sixth schedule to this Act shall be deemed to be adulterated within the meaning of this Act.
It is also provided that the word ' maple ' shall not be used, either alone or in combination with any other word or words, on a package containing any article of food which is not pure maple sugar or pure maple syrup.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Before the Orders of the Day
are called, I desire to correct a statement which I made in this House on January 20 last in the debate on the Address. Upon that occasion I directed the attention of the House to an article which had appeared in the Montreal Daily Telegraph, and which had been reproduced in the Daily Chronicle of London under the caption, ' Frenzied Finance in Canada.' I said that the article in question had been written by or under the direction of my predecessor, the ex-Minister of Finance. It has been drawn to my attention that the article to which I referred appeared in the Montreal Daily Telegraph a few days before the Hon. Mr. Fielding assumed its management. I therefore take very much pleasure in correcting the statement I then made, and in saying that in attributing to the exMinister of Finance the article in question, or in stating that it was written under his direction, I was in error as to the facts.

Mr. PAQUET moved;
For copies of all correspondence, memoranda and other papers concerning the inspection of immigrants entering Canada from the moral, intellectual and physical standpoints.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in connection with this motion for copies of all correspondence, memoranda and other papers, concerning the inspection from the moral, intellectual and physical standpoint of immigrants entering Canada, I would like to offer a few remarks. My only object in doing so, is to ensure a more thorough inspection of those people who seek admittance into the Canadian household.
In every province of Canada, we have thousands of acres of land of unexceptional quality. We are in need of farmers and farm labourers to put under crop our unoccupied lands, so as to increase our output and increase our national wealth. The development of our trade, our industries and our agriculture has drawn to our shores, in the [DOT]course of the last fiscal year, 402,432 immigrants. In the interest of our civilization, we are anxious to make a wise selection of those who are to be admitted into the Canadian family circle. The enormous increase in the number of immigrants has a tendency to fill the country with heterogeneous elements difficult to assimilate.
Race assimilation, in this immense and young country of ours, is a social problem
*of the greatest moment. The population of the United States reaches 100,000,000 souls. However, Mr. Hanotaux, in his fine book 'La France vivante,' writes; 'The American people is not as yet an actual entity; it cannot be stated with absolute-truth that an American ideal is outstanding.' It is a common sense notion, which the experience of centuries confirms, that the less homogeneous the population the greater the difficulties in the way of the government. We have to solve the1 appal- . king problem of governing with order and success the various races congregated on the Canadian soil, with aspirations and traditions brought from the United States, Europe or Asia.
If we are anxious to carry out the national ideal and to ensure the unity of the Canadian people, we should study with the greatest care the problem of race assimilation in this Dominion. Oriental immigration has just been in this House a subject of debate. Accordingly I shall forego any references to the yellow or Oriental peril. If we are anxious to safeguard our institutions, if we wish to maintain the bonds which unite the various provinces of Canada, it would be the part of wisdom to close the doors of Canada to immigrants who would, be unable to understand our manners, our traditions and our past. I am chary of those new comers who are not likely to grasp the lofty, far-seeing aims of the fathers of Confederation. They might bring ruin to that splendid monument erected in 1867.
We should welcome agricultural immigrants. The tiller of the soil is aware that in ,a new country gifted with a suitable climate he will be in a position to follow his calling. We should be careful as regards the industrial class. Their turn of mind will incline them to settle in large centres, where they will be confronted with competition of a more or less pronounced type, such as exists in the country they come from. The industrial classes flock towards cities, but there they will not find such scope, such opportunities, as the virgin soil of our unoccupied lands offers to settlers of the agricultural class. The flow of immigration which is constantly growing from year to year fills our cities with thousands and thousands of people, who, on account of their straitened pecuniary circumstances, crowd together in houses where sanitary requirements iare too often neglected. The bulk of those immigrants are constantly shifting from house to house, from one neighbourhood to the other, and from town to town, as well.

They are too often indifferent to sanitary requirements and constantly at variance with them. The provision of the Act for their deportation within two years after their landing, whenever they develop tuberculosis, is of very doubtful efficiency, on account of the unsatisfactory control which under present conditions it is possible to exert over such matters. So I say we should be thankful to the Government for specially assisting the immigration of farmers and farm labourers. The bulk of settlers should be of the agricultural class.
According to the last census, the proportion of Canadian-born was equivalent to 77.9 per cent of the population, and supplied 50.5 per cent of criminals. British subjects bom outside Canada made up 11.6 per cent of the population, and. supplied 15.3 per cent of criminals. People coming from the United States represented 4.2 per cent of the population and 5.8 per cent of convicted criminals. People originating from other countries represented 6.2 per cent of the population, and supplied 12.2 per cent of the criminals. People born outside Canada represented 22.1 per cent of the population, and were responsible for 49-5 per cent of criminals. During the fiscal year 1910-11, 1,004 criminals were Canadian-born, and 861 foreign-bom.
I must emphasize the great influence exerted by heredity in the spread of lunacy. If there exists a well established law it is that of hereditary transmission of disease. Ancestral deficiencies are transmitted from generation to generation; a large proportion of the descendants of a lunatic, a criminal, a man of unbalanced mind, will themselves be deficient in those respects. Mr. L. Brown, a New York representative at the congress, points out the case of the Juke family, five generations of which have given 200 criminals, including . seven murderers and hundreds of men and women unable to honestly earn a living. We too often read accounts of series of tragic occurrences wherein immigrants play the leading .parts. These things are recurring more and more frequently in large cities, and the authorities should take more efficient means towards ridding us of such criminals.
The means resorted to at present are unavailing. I have looked into the form which the immigrant is required to fill and I see it contains no reference whatever to moral qualities. To my mind, we should deport all those whose previous record cannot be shown to be good. There should 'be some sort of agreement between the Dominion Government and foreign governments towards satisfactorily settling the question 
of inspection of immigrants as to their moral standing.
Every immigrant should be called upon to show a penal certificate under the signature of the provincial or municipal authorities. Any immigrant who is anxious for admittance into the Canadian household should have a certificate showing that he has committed no crime implying moral turpitude. Such certificate might he issued by a magistrate, a clergyman or the mayor of the municipality wherein the immigrant resides.
Were such a provision incorporated in our statutes, we should 'have at our disposal a new means of ridding Canada of criminals. Steamship companies should be obliged to furnish a certificate as to the moral standing of every immigrant. The provisions of our statute relative to deportation of undesirables enables us to do away with criminals. But too often no action can be taken until some further crime has been committed.
Deportation is the sending back to the country they have come from, of immigrants disheartened by grief, sorely disappointed just when they were on the point of conquering freedom in this Dominion. To-day the British authorities seem disposed to cooperate with the Dominion authorities towards ensuring >a better choice of immigrants. We should take advantage of these dispositions.
Previous to 1903, undesirable immigrants could easily enough gain admittance into this country. In 1903, under an immigration Act, there was a system of inspection of immigrants in our seaports organized by the Dominion authorities. In 1912, 147,000 immigrants landed at Quebec. We have there an inspection board which does excellent work. I could not praise too highly the knowledge and zeal of Dr. Page, with a view to improving and perfecting the system of inspection for immigrants.
On several occasions, the hon. member for the St. Lawrence division of Montreal strongly urged the inspection of immigrants at their starting point. In that way would the necessity of deporting undesirables be avoided with its consequent inconveniences. The former Minister of the Interior spoke as follows on May 14, 1910:
I agree that an inspection effected on the other side would offer great advantages, hut for the time being it cannot be carried out. This Government has no jurisdiction outside the limits of the Dominion and our inspectors would be without the requisite powers.
We have no jurisdiction over foreign territory, but an agreement might be con-

eluded with the authorities of the various countries.
Ret me quote the following extract from the report of the United States Immigration Commission. It might help towards solving the problem of the inspection of immigrants:
It is highly desirable both for humanitarian and medical reasons that aliens who are not admissible to the United States should be turned hack at foreign ports of embarkation, or, better still, that they should not leave their homes for such ports only to be returned. It has been strongly urged by immigration officials and other students of the question that the embarkation at foreign ports of persons not admissible to the United States because of their physical condition would be more effectually prevented by a medical inspection by American officers at such ports. This plan was so strongly urged that this Government a few years ago made official inquiry respecting the probable attitude of European Governments toward it. At that time one or two governments expressed a willingness to permit such an inspection by American officials; others made indefinite replies to the inquiry, while others were positively opposed.
As >a matter of fact, United States officials *have been carrying on the medical inspection of immigrants in the ports of Italy for the last ten years and their recommendations have in every case been accepted by the steamship companies.
Steamship companies should strictly be held responsible for the proper inspection of immigrants. Managers of such companies should be made to understand in unmistakable terms that they must not take over to Canada undesirable immigrants. To-day companies are obliged to repatriate at their expense immigrants which cannot be admitted. But, to my mind, repatriation 'by the steamship company does not constitute a sufficiently severe penalty. The payment of a heavy fine should also be exacted. In that way will the steamship companies realize that they must have passengers undergo a searching medical examination at the sailing port.
Immigrants bound for the United States must undergo medical examination at the .sailing ports. Those regulations are more or less strictly adhered to according to the country and the steamship company. The latter has an interest in transporting only desirable immigrants. Should it take over to the United States undesirables, it is forced to take them hack at its own expense and even a fine may be exacted by the officials.
The Austro-Ameriean company which transports produce from Greece, was compelled, in connection with the first trips *effected by its ships, to repatriate at its expense 300 immigrants bound for the
United States. In the meantime that company has had recourse to the services of several medical men in the various parts of Greece. Every Greek who wishes to emigrate to the United States is called upon to undergo medical inspection in a Green city. If the outcome is satisfactory, the doctor issues a certificate to the immigrant who proceeds to the sailing point. There he must undergo a final examination. Thanks to the introduction of that system, there is no occasion for repatriating undesirable immigrants. The inspection is performed as a rule by a medical officer in the employ of the steamship company. In some of the ports the United States consul appoints the medical inspector, who is paid by the company.
At Naples, Palermo and Messina, the American and Italian authorities have concluded an agreement. The inspection is effected by the officers of the American hospitals .and health department. Their dealings in the matter have no official character, but their suggestions are always accepted. Those officers are also supposed to look into the sanitary conditions of the steamers carrying the immigrants.
German authorities take great precautions in regard to the immigrants coming from Austria and Russia and who must pass through Germany to reach the seaports. Inspection stations have been established at the frontier. Undesirables are not permitted to reach the seaports.
It is surprising to see what space is occupied in Italian periodicals by questions relating to immigration. Private associations for the protection of immigrants are very numerous. Italy has an immigration code which is a work of no mean importance.
A doctor of the Italian Royal Navy of good reputation accompanies the immigrants on the ship which is to transport thorn. He is expected to .board the ship two days previous to departure, and to remain on hoard until its return. The doctor concerns himself with safeguarding the immigrant as much as possible against sharpers. That officer bears the title of ' Royal Commissioner ' and is of great assistance to immigrants.
I have furnished those particulars to show what measures should be taken towards perfecting our legislation concerning immigrants. With the oo-operation of the British authorities, we might make an experiment .and see what results would be obtained from a system of inspection in a few sailing ports.
The ideal system would consist in an

inspection effected on the ship 'by a medical man appointed and paid by the Canadian Government. That medical officer would have all the time requisite to make a thorough examination. I trust the bon. Minister of the Interior will introduce that system on some of the ships. That system of inspection strikes me as necessary, in cases especially where we have to do with immigrants suffering from diseases of the mind.
Under certain circumstances, the medical officer at the port either of departure or of arrival, will not be able in a few minutes' time to determine the mental condition of an immigrant. The mental inspection of immigrants is a question of much concern to our neighbours. They are getting anxious over the constantly increasing number of those who have to be confined to asylums. In the state of New York, such asylums contain 13,163 lunatics of foreign origin, entailing an expenditure of nearly $4,000,000. I could not insist too much on the great part played by heredity in the spreading of lunacy.
Mental inspection constitutes from the social standpoint one of the gravest aspects of this immigration question. The specialist in mental diseases in our large cities is in a position to make us realize the great necessity of that inspection. Deficients and feeble-minded persons are too frequently admitted in our country. Oftentimes they become criminals, patrons of our jails and hospitals. Should they remain at large, then their descendants will bear the imprint of degeneracy, and may become a burden to the State.
I call on the Minister of the Interior to appoint a specialist in mental diseases as inspector of immigrants in our seaports. Such an officer would certainly be of great service to society.
In 1910, I entered my protest against section 4 of the Act, which enables the minister to issue a permit in writing under which a person may enter Canada without subjecting to the requirements of the law. Such a permit should not, from the social and economic viewpoint, be granted in other than the exceptional cases provided in the Act.
It too often happens that transportation companies consider the immigration question solely as a means of securing some revenue. The assimilation of the various races whose immigrants are flowing into Canada is a problem of the greatest moment. Formerly the strong, robust inhabitants of Northern and Western Europe emigrated in large numbers to the United States. In

latter years, these conditions have undergone a change. The inhabitants of Southern and Eastern Europe are invading the United States.
In 1912, the United States received 40,408 English, 14,578 Scotch, 157,134 Italians, 162,239 Russian and 178,875 Austro-Hungarian immigrants.
In the course of the last fiscal year, Canada received 150,542 British, 21,875 Austro-Hungarians, 16,601 Italians and 18,623 immigrants from the United States.
I prefer our immigration to that which goes to the United States. Our immigrants come largely from Northern Europe, the British Isles and the United States and have a better insight into the working of British institutions than have the immigrants from Southern Europe. On our shoulders rests the burden of establishing European civilization within our immense territory. To attain that object we put severe strictures on the introduction of undesirables.
On January 23, 1914, the hon. member for Strathcona (Mr. Douglas) said: I notice that in spite of the strong current of American immigration directed towards Canada within the last five years, Canada has gained 20,000 only. I wish to have those figures recorded in ' Hansard '.

It will be noticed that there is a yearly increase in the numbers of those coming to Canada, as well as in the numbers of those going to the United States. I made a special study of those statistics which are rather a matter of surprise to me. According to my figuring, during the fiscal year 1010-11, 44,439 Canadian crossed over the border to settle permanently in the United States. During the fiscal year 1911-12, that figure went up to 42,649.
Those so different calculations show the importance of improving our statistics.

Would the hon. member permit me to ask a question for the mere sake of information? Could he find out how many of those 42,000 immigrants who went through to the United States during the year mentioned, had left our country in order to settle finally in the United States,

and how many of them intended to come hack to Canada?

I stated that on the 20th of last January the hon. member for Strath-cona (Mr. Douglas) said that Canada had increased her population but by 20,000 in the space of six years, because 549,919 people had gone from Canada to the United States, while 616,212 had come from the United States to Canada. I made researches and I found that during the fiscal year just alluded to, 44,439 Canadians who had been residing here for quite a few years had gone to the United States in order to settle there permanently. During the same period 25,000 Canadians have returned from the United States in order to settle here definitely.
I shall now conclude my remarks. I have had another resolution put on the Orders of the Day to the effect that a commission should be appointed with the object of studying the question of European immigration, including the question of repatriation and that of French, British and Belgian immigration. I intend to deal with this matter again, if I only oan, at another phase of the session. Moreover, some inquisitive minds, with conscientiousness and patience, may continue this task in a debate which must rank above political party considerations.
Trying to improve our legislation with respect to immigration; trying to preserve our national character, is to show that we hold Canada, our country, in pious and faithful veneration.

speechtext:
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Paquet) who has moved the resolution, himself being a medical man, has quite properly discussed the question largely from the standpoint of good citizenship, and has emphasized the need of a proper medical examination of all immigrants coming to make their homes in Canada. It is a question of very great importance from the standpoint of the individual as well as from that of the state. While I was not able to follow the hon. gentleman in his speech, as it was in a language with which I am not familiar, still I understand that he has particularly emphasized the need of a more stringent carrying out of our present regulations regarding the admittance of immigrants into Canada.
Our immigration law at the present time is fairly rigid; but, as with all other laws, exceptions are made at times in connection with its enforcement: that is, in the enforcement of this or any other Act there may be
times and occasions when the strict regulations are not lived up to, and as a result undoubtedly some undesirable immigrants, notwithstanding all the precautions that may be taken, gain access to our country. Our immigration laws at the present time provide for the exclusion of all immigrants who are physically, mentally or morally unsuited for our country. Those who are encouraged to come to Canada, being able to pass the medical examination and the other requirements of our law, are of the agricultural classes and domestic servants. For these classes bonuses are paid, and the energies of our officers are largely directed to getting a sufficient number of these desirable classes. By reason of the fact that this is an agricultural country, we are very anxious to get in as many as possible to occupy the land, and that is the reason for the special propaganda in that direction.
The examination that immigrants have to undergo has been much more rigid during the last few years than it was some years ago. Not only have we more stringent laws regarding their admittance into Canada, but we have a more strict enforcement of those laws than our neighbours south of the international boundary line. On my way to the old country last year, I had the privilege of stopping off for a day at New York, and I visited Ellis Island. I had the opportunity of seeing the medical men there passing upon the immigrants seeking access to America, and it was a very interesting proceeding. I also had the opportunity of discussing the question w'th the Commissioner of Immigration of the United States, a gentleman of independent means, who is devoting his time and attention to the work by reason of his love for it. He admitted that we were getting a considerably better class of immigrants into Canada than they were into the United States. This was something that I was rather pleased to hear, although as a Canadian I was quite satisfied in my own mind that it was the case, but it comes with more force when emphasized by a commissioner of immigration of a neighbouring country. With regard to the southern European immigrants he declared that there was no comparison; that those they were getting were not at all the equal of those we were getting in Canada..
We have inspection in the motherland first by the British Board of Trade officers. This examination, I may say, is rather imperfect; still it is an examination. Then there is an examination by the steamship company's medical officer before the immigrants come

on board; and an examination is made by the steamship medical officer on the ship on the way across the ocean, when he has an opportunity of coming into closer contact with the immigrants. In addition to that, we have the examination by our own medical officers before the immigrants land in Canada. The examination made by the steamship company's medical officer in the old country is of very great importance, and the steamship companies in their own interest are honestly endeavouring to admit on their steamships coming to Canada no one who cannot pass the requisite medical examination, because the law imposes the penalty upon the steamship companies of having such immigrants deported at the expense of the steamship companies if they have not exercised due precaution. It is true that the examination which takes place when the immigrants are going on board ship,is of a somewhat cursory character; but during the week they are on board the vessel the medical officer has an opportunity of coming closer in touch with them and of seeing any outbreak of disease that may occur.
Within the last three week's I had an opportunity of discussing the question with the representatives of the steamship companies, and I brought to their attention that they had been accused in the past of not having a sufficiently critical medical examination of the immigrants coming into Canada; that as a result during the past year we have had more deportations than in any previous year. They might have answered by stating that we had a very much larger number of immigrants coming to Canada this year than in any previous year. At the same time it is another evidence that our Canadian medical officers are doing their duty , more completely than they did some years ago. Still, the fact that the steamship companies had not detected these cases seemed to be a reflection upon them. One complaint which was made to me, and which I think was touched upon by my hon. friend who preceded me (Mr. Paquet), was that the medical men on board the steamships were not paid sufficient salaries to keep them in their positions permanently; that young physicians, just after graduating from college, secured positions with those companies for the sake of the experience and that they were paid such pittances that they did not remain there for any length of time. The steamship companies said that that accusation might justly have been charged against them some years ago, (but that they did not

think it could truthfully be laid at their door at the present time, inasmuch as they had raised the salaries of, and were keeping these medical officers permanently in their positions. While there is undoubtedly room for improvement, and while improvements are being made from time to time still I am glad to say that the examination is of a much more successful and critical character than it was before.
Suggestions are constantly being made in regard to immigration, and we are willing and ever ready to adopt suggestions which we think are practical and in the interest of our country, because I am sure that we are all desirous of seeing not only quantity but quality in the immigrants that come to Canada, in order that we may build up a strong Canadian nationality.
The hon. member has also discussed the question of the Canadian Government paying a doctor to take his position on those steamships in order to have a sufficiently competent examination. I discussed that question also with the steamship companies. I told them that that suggestion had been made to me before but that I did not think it was necessary for the Government of Canada to come to the succour of these wealthy steamship companies in order to give sufficient compensation to their medical officers. They agreed with me in that respect, seeing that the law states that steamship companies must provide competent medical men on their steamships. Now they are doing so without the Government of Canada being asked to come to their relief.
The Immigration Act is very rigid in regard to immigrants who come to our country. I might take the time to place upon ' Hansard ' sections 27, 28 and 29, which read as follows:
27.	Before any passengers are permitted to leave a vessel in Canada the immigration officer in charge, or any officer directed by him, may go on hoard and inspect such vessel and examine and take extracts from the manifest of passengers, and from the bill of health.
The master shall permit any examination of passengers required under this Act to be made on board his vessel whenever so directed by the immigration officer in charge.
28.	Medical officers appointed under this Act shall make a physical and mental examination of all immigrants and passengers seeking to land in Canada from any ship or vessel, except in the case of Canadian citizens and persons who have Canadian domicile. Such examination shall be made in accordance with and subject to regulations prescribed by the superintendent of immigration under the direction or with the approval of the minister.
29.	The immigration officer in charge, after satisfying himself that the requirements of

this Act, and of any Order Council, proclamation or regulation made thereunder, have been carried out, shall grant written permission to the master of the vessel to allow the passengers to leave the vessel.
These are the particular provisions in regard to the medical examination of immigrants just before they land in Canada. The steamship companies themselves are under obligations to deport at their own expense all undesirable immigrants that are brought to Canada by reason of negligence on their part.
It is therefore necessary to enforce the law as strictly as possible, otherwise they would be subject to sub-clauses 8 and 9 of section 23, which read:
8.	Any transportation company or person knowingly and wilfully landing, or assisting to land or attempting to land in Canada, any prohibited immigrant or person whose entry into Canada has been forbidden under this Act, shall be guilty of an offence and shall be liable on conviction, to a fine of not more than five hundred dollars and not less than fifty dollars for each prohibited immigrant or other person so landed in Canada, or whose landing in Canada was so attempted.
9.	Any transportation company or person interfering with or resisting an immigration officer in the performance of his duty under this Act, or knowingly and wilfully assisting in the escape of any person detained by an officer, or at an immigrant station for any purpose under this Act, or giving false information to an officer, whereby such officer is induced to land or permit the landing of any person in Canada who otherwise would be refused landing, for any cause under this Act or would be detained for examination, shall be guilty of an offence and shall be liable to a fine of not more than five hundred dollars and not less than twenty dollars for each such offence.
I; has been suggested, time after time, that we should have an examination at the port of departure of the immigrants, to the exclusion of the examination in Canada. Australia has adopted that principle quite recently, and how it will work out we do not know, but we are watching the experiment with a great deal of interest. While that system may be applicable to Australia, it possibly might not be applicable to Canada, for Australia is several weeks sail from England, while Canada is only seven or eight days, and it would be severe on the steamship companies if it were provided that they should at their own expense carry back undesirable immigrants from Australia. We have, at present, a certain medical examination conducted by the British Board of Trade on the other side; we have an examination conducted by the steamship companies by their own officers, and we nave the medical
men on the steamships. If all these precautions are properly enforced they would, in my opinion, constitute a pretty reliable safeguard against undesirable immigrants coming to this country.
It is much more difficult, of course, to get to know the moral character of immigrants than it is to determine on their physical and mental state. Our officials in the old country, if they become aware that any person is coming to Canada whose character is not good, or wbo has been convicted of crime, are required to notify our agents in Canada with the greatest expediency, so that such persons may be deported. Should any such escape the vigilant eyes of our officers, we have a provision that undesirable immigrants may be deported within three years after coming to Canada, and if during these three years we find an immigrant is physically, mentally, or morally unfit to make a good and healthy citizen, we can have that immigrant depoTted. The requirement that during the winter season an immigrant shall have $50, and during the summer months $25, before being allowed to land, is a guarantee against our getting an over-supply of people who might become a public charge. We aTe not encouraging general artisans to come to Canada, unless they have assured employment before leaving home.
I can assure my hon. friend that repatriation has not been lost sight of by the immigration authorities. We have our colonization agents, our repatriation agents, and our boundary inspectors. We have agents visiting the New England States, to which so many of our French people have migrated, to engage in work in the mills there. Many of them go temporarily for a few months in the year, coming back to Canada and living here for the greater part of the twelve months, while some of them have become permanent residents in the States. To encourage these people to come back, not only to the province of Quebec but to induce as many as possible to occupy our lands in the Canadian Northwest, we have officers engaged, who I think are doing most valuable work. I was glad to hear my hon. friend approve of the repatriation work conducted by these officers.
The hon. gentleman has suggested that we should have some expert in mental diseases, and as to that I may point out that we are encouraging our officers at the principle ports to visit the United States centres, to gain as much experience as possible, not only as to the ment'd examina-

tion of immigrants, but also as to their physical examination. Dr. Page, our Quebec agent, is a gentleman of high professional attainment, and he has recently returned from a trip to the United States, during -which he looked into the system of examination with regard to the mentally unsound. That is a practice which should be followed in connection with our principal physicians in the various ports, in order that they may keep themselves in touch *with the most modern method of examination. I am anxious to see the examination work perfected as much as possible, and I am taking as much personal interest in it as the time from my other duties will permit. I have no objection whatever to the resolution being passed, and I am sure the thanks of the House are due to my hon. friend for bringing this important matter to our attention, arid to the attention of the country.
Motion agreed to.	.

That in the opinion of this House, the federal Government ought to encourage the projected international exhibition on the occasion of the fiftieth anniversary of the establishment of confederation.
He said: In moving this resolution I feel that I am conveying to the Government and to this House the wishes of many of the most prominent public bodies, and of many of the leading citizens of Canada. I am actuated personally by no partisan feeling; I intend to speak only as a Canadian who has the welfare of his country at heart. I am, I believe, voicing a sentiment, which has been gaining strength of late, irrespective of province, of party, of creed, -or of race. Three years hence, on the first of July, 1917, we will celebrate the fiftieth anniversary of Canadian Confederation. It is a day well worthy of being remembered, not only in North America, and not only in the British Empire, of which we are a component part, but in all the world.
Our constitution may not be perfect, nor do I believe there is any instrument of government in this wide world that is perfect. No human law is perfect, but every one must admit that the constitution of Canada, the system of government under which we live, compares very favourably with that of other nations. Indeed, during the last few years, we have seen the great [DOT] commonwealth of Australia, our sister

dominion, and also the new-born union of South Africa, taking their inspiration, and drawing the vital principles of their government from the constitution given us by the Fathers of our Confederation. In Great Britain itself, where political economists are to-day discussing a system of devolution which would harmonize the various parts of the United Kingdom, they point to Canada as an example of a country carried on under the best system of federative government. The year 1867 is, therefore, all-inspiring to Canadian students of history. It is an outstanding date; it is a landmark in the field of Canadian history. Confederation-and let me say here, I do not intend to deliver a First of July oration-was the culmination of several unsuccessful attempts to establish a firm government in Canada. We all know, and you, Mr. Speaker, and others of the older generation in this House know better than most men, that the vastness of our country, the varied races composing our population, the conflicts of interests along our frontier of four thousand miles extending from one coast to another, made the problem of Confederation in 1867 a most complex and difficult one. Yet, if we look back, we cannot help but see that the process of nation building in Canada has been a gradual one, that the extension of the principle of responsible government has gone on step by step and that its several stages have come in due time in our history. It may be that as we read the annals of our constitutional government we shall find some gaps from time to time; but every British subject knows full well that it is the custom of Great Britain to gradually educate the subjects of the Crown in self-government.
The successive constitutions given to Canada answered very fully the needs of the day; since the cessation of the French domination, when the subjects of His Majesty the King of France were governed by a bureaucratic oligarchy, each period under British domination in Canada has marked an advance and always with this guiding principle-that our constitution should as far as possible be similar to that of the mother country. Taking a brief survey of our constitutional history, I find that from the very beginning it has been the policy of the statesmen in England to assimilate our political institutions to those of the mother country.
Let me give you a few dates and a few facts. With 1759 we reach the end of the French regime in Canada. In 1763, on

the 10th of February, the formal cession of Canada to Great Britain took place by the Treaty of Paris. On the 7th of October of that year, we have the first embryonic constitution of the country. It is contained in the famous proclamation oi General Murray. By that proclamation four governments were established within the British possessions in North America: One in Quebec, one in Bast Florida, one in West Florida and one in Grenada. This _ proclamation initiated what is known to historians as the Military Regime. There was then no popular assembly given to the King's new subjects, and quite a chaotic period ensued. The laws of Great Britain were substituted for the laws which had been in force during the French regime. The new subjects of His Majesty, who were then the vast majority in Canada, petitioned the King for a new constitution. It was then that Lord North introduced in the British Parliament what is known as the Quebec Act of 1774. The Quebec Act is considered by my fellow-countrymen, and ought to be considered by every true Canadian, as the Magna Charta of this country. By it the Canadians of the day -and they were mostly of French origin- were guaranteed the free exercise of their religion, the clergy their accustomed dues; property and civil rights were again brought under the old French laws and customs which had existed in the country; the criminal law of Great Britain, the most humane and generous of that time, was* introduced in the colony. The Act also provides for the establishment of a council composed of members selected by the Crown, to legislate for the colony. Shortly afterwards the revolt of the Thirteen Colonies broke out, and our forefathers loyal to the Crown witnessed the arrival in Canada of those sturdy sons of Great Britain known as the United Empire Loyalists. These United Empire loyalists ha>d been accustomed in the Thirteen Colonies to freedom and self-government. They would not tolerate any longer the irresponsible control of the executive council, and they in their turn petitioned for a popular assembly, and the Imperial Parliament, naturally, logically, enacted the famous Act of 1791, known as the Constitutional Act. Briefly, this Act divided Canada into two provinces, Upper Canada and Lower Canada, each with a legislative assembly and with a legislative council elected for life and selected by the Crown.
But the executive council was independent of the assembly, and when there was a deadlock between the executive and the assembly, the only remedy oi the assembly was to Tefuse Supply. This constitution, though imperfect, was a considerable improvement upon the two constitutions which had previously been granted to this country by Great Britain. As Lord Granville says in his memoirs:
The object of this Act was to conform the constitution of Canada with that of Great Britain as nearly as the differences arising- from the manners of the people and from the present circumstances of the provinces will admit.
As I said a moment ago, the tendency' of Great Britain has always been to give to her dominions constitutions similar, so far as possible, to that of the mother country. The constitution of 1791 lasted until 1840. I need not refer to the troubles which, prior to 1840, occurred in different parts of the country. It is admitted today that the men who fought in Upper Canada and in Lower Canada had but one object in view: that of maintaining the best traditions of British Government, and of obtaining for this young country a full measure of responsible government. The mother country sent to Canada one of her most gifted sons, in the person of Lord Durham. At first his mission was stifled through jealousies which existed in the party to which he belonged, but, seen in the light of history, much as we differ from some of his conclusions, the report which he made on that occasion remains as one of the greatest state papers of the nineteenth century. Upon that report the constitution given to Canada in 1840 was based. The main characteristic of this third constitution was that responsible government was at length granted; Her Majesty's Government in Canada was responsible to the people of Canada, and not to the home authorities. Previously, while legislative powers were given to the provinces, responsible government was withheld, and the only recourse the people had when their grievances became acute was to refuse supply. Lord Durham had said that it was not possible to secure harmony in any other way than by administering the Government on those principles which had been found to be perfectly efficacious in Great Britain, and while he would not impair a single prerogative of the Crown, and while he believed that the interests of the people of these provinces required the protection of prerogatives which had not hitherto been exercised, still, the



Crown should submit to the necessary consequences of representative institutions.
Then we reach the fourth period, that of Confederation in 1867. I need not recite to you, Mr. Speaker, or to the House, the struggles which, under the union, brought about the deadlocks so frequently in ine fifties, but they form one of the most interesting pages of our Canadian history. The double majority system, the cry of representation by population, may have precipitated the crisis, but it must be borne [DOT] in mind that from the beginning of British domination in Canada the idea of a union of the various British provinces in North America had been advocated not only in Canada but in Great Britain as well. Indeed, Chief Justice Smith of Quebec, at the end of the eighteenth century, later on Chief Justice Sewell, and Lord Durham himself, had advocated the federal system as the best means of harmonizing all conditions in His Majesty's dominions. In the Quebec resolutions are clearly expressed the leading principles on which the Canadian federation rests-which, in my judgment, deserve to be commemorated on the fiftieth anniversary of that event- federation, with a central government having jurisdiction over matters of common interest to the whole country comprised in the union, and a number of provincial governments having the control and management of certain local matters naturally and conveniently belonging to them, each government being administered in accordance with the well-understood principles of the British system of parliamentary institutions.
Two facts are prominently outstanding m the various circumstances to which I have briefly referred, especially in the last instrument of government given to Canada by the mother country. One is the insistence of the Canadian representatives upon the principle of maintaining intact our British connection with the mother country, and the other is the principle of self-government for Canada. Under our constitution, 'Canadians -are loyal subjects of His Majesty the King of Great Britain; yet Canada is mistress in her own house. As a student of history and political economy, I find that this is the miracle which alone could be accomplished by British statesmanship.
Sir, many were the apprehensions in 1867 as to the ultimate destiny of our young country. Some predicted the absorption of Canada by the United States, our great neighbour. Others foresaw the dislocation
IMr. I .emieux.]
of our various provinces. There were even statesmen in England who shared these pessimistic views. But we have survived all those fears, all those predictions, all those forebodings. The Canadian Confederation is now fast approaching its semi-centennial, with a Canada united, hopeful and above all conscious of her national existence within the great empire. A mere geographical expression fifty years ago, our country is now known, respected, envied, not only in the British Empire but all over the world. Indeed, our trials were many since 1867. We had to quell two rebellions in the West. The lean and long years of fiscal vexations on the part of Washington were deeply felt and resented in- Canada. We also followed with a longing eye the trail, the long trail, of our young men going southward, lured as they were by the glamour of American industrial centres during many years. The conflicts of jurisdiction between the Provinces and the Central Government were at times very serious. We [DOT] had our full share of racial and religious difficulties, and we also, during many years, felt how uncertain would be the settlement of the great lone land of the West. But, Mr. Speaker, better days have come. Canada has emerged, hopeful, vigorous, united, from the crucial test. Need I repeat the words used by the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) on one occasion-words that are repeated all over the world?: 'If the nineteenth century was the century of the United States, the twentieth will be Canada's century.' Let me quote the remarks made not long ago by the hon. gentleman who leads the House (Mr. Borden). The right hon. gentleman said:
The highest future for this Dominion lies within the British Empire, upon conditions of equal status. .	. Its flag streams in undiminished splendour upon the breezes of the 20th century, and mindful of its power for peace and its influence for civilization and humanity, we do not dare to doubt its greater destiny in the years to come.
Sir, the thoughts expressed so admirably by both the leaders of the House are also the thoughts of the seven and one-half million Canadians who inhabit this country. It is the general belief that the twentieth century will witness the full development of Canada. Is it not, then, fitting and proper that we 5 p.m. should commemorate the event upon which, more than all others, rests our great future as a country? Confederation has not only

supplied us with a stimulus to our political development, but Confederation has achieved for us a great material develop' ment. Canada extends now over half a continent. To quote again the language used by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister:
Do you realize how great a country Canada is? If you could pivot Canada upon its eastern seaboard, it would cover the northern part of the Atlantic ocean, the British Islands, Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Holland, Belgium, the northern part of France the entire German Empire, and a considerable part of European Russia, and a man who lives in Halifax is a thousand miles farther away from Victoria than he is from London.
Canada has one-third of the area of the British Empire; her area is one-third of that of Africa, and one-fifth of that of Asia. Canada is larger in area than the United States, including Alaska. Canada is as large as thirty United Kingdoms and eighteen Germanys; twice the size of British India; almost as large as Europe; eighteen times the size of France; thirty-three times the size of Italy. We have carved since Confederation, three provinces out of the prairies of the West; and I believe, with the right hon. leader of the Opposition and my friends from the West, that there is yet another province to be carved out of the Peace River valley district. The population of Canada is increasing at the rate of one thousand per day. The trade of Canada in 1913 reached the high-water mark. It is over one billion. It has doubled in ten years and trebled in fifteen years. We own the greatest farming territory in the world. Our forest, our mines, our fisheries, contain inexhaustible wealth. Our industrial development in the last ten years was the greatest on record. Our railway mileage in 1867 was 2,278 miles, and in 1913 it was 29,304 miles. We will soon have three transcontinental railways spanning the country from one ocean to the other.
The object of the proposed commemoration of the establishment of Confederation is, in my judgment, twofold. It will tell the world of the triumph of our political institutions and also of the signal success of our material development. It would meet the approval of all Canadians, because	nobody to-day questions the
wisdom	of * the Confederation Act.
Sir John A. Macdonald, Sir George Cartier, George Brown, Oliver Mowat, Alexander Mackenzie, all joined in the great constitutional struggle, and this celebration would therefore meet with the approval of all 92*
their political heirs. It would attract the attention of the world to the potential wealth of Canada. It would bind more closely the East and the West, for notwithstanding Rudyard Kipling, Mr. Speaker, there is an East and there is a West. It would make Canadians realize their vast heritage, and it would Show what a large place we occupy in the British Empire.	I might be astved
at Ibis juncture, ' Why commemorate the semi-centennial?' I answer without any hesitation that in America and Canada we move faster than in any other country. A semi-centennial in Canada is worth a centennial in Europe. The idea itself was launched in Montreal, in the month of October last by an enterprising journalist, the editor of La Presse, one of the largest dailies in Canada; but the idea had been in the public mind for a long time before that and the journalist was only giving expression to the general sentiment. A largely attended meeting of the citizens of Montreal was called in October; and after speeches had been delivered by public men from both parties, and by gentlemen occupying very high positions in. the commercial and the financial activities of Montreal, resolutions were adopted. The press, generally, has favoured the project. I just wish to quote a few lines from a letter written by the originator of the project to Sir Hugh Graham, editor of the Montreal Star:
Montreal, November 26, 1913. Honourable Sir:
As you know, there has been considerable talk about holding an international exhibition in Canada in 1917, 'IS or '19, to commemorate the fiftieth anniversary of Confederation. VVe ourselves are heartily in favour of the scheme, and from investigations, we have conducted find that public opinion throughout Canada is unanimous in approval of the project. Already over a thousand interviews with some of the most prominent citizens of Montreal and other cities and towns throughout Quebec province, have been published; the mayors of all the principal cities of Canada have been asked their views by telegraph, and in every case they have endorsed the idea and promised their hearty support, while the Prime Ministers of several provinces have also expressed their approval.
To which Sir Hugh Graham, inter alia,
replied:
That the idea of an international exhibition meets the approval of many Canadians and of many friends of Canada, has been well shown by the expressions of approval secured, not only in this country, but in Great Britain. The endorsements of the mayors of most of the cities of the Dominion, which have been sent to you, coupled with the assurances of sympathy which

have been cabled over by our London correspondent since the suggestion was first broached in England, would seem to indicate that the project of an international exhibition in Canada in 1917 or one of the succeeding years, appeal strongly to all those who have the welfare of the Dominion at heart. In the last few weelcs the proposal has been endorsed by Lord Strathcona, Earl Grey, Lord Desborough, Sir Thomas Skinner, Mr. A. G. Smithers, chairman of the Grand Trunk railway; Mr. Bur-bridge, manager of Harrod's stores; Sir Trevor Dawson, of Vickers-Maxim, and some three hundred of the leading manufacturers of London, Liverpool, Manchester, Birmingham, Sheffield, Leeds. Bradford, Halifax, Hull. Bristol, Glasgow, Aberdeen, Dundee and Belfast. With such support in Great Britain, it seems to me we would be neglecting our duty if we did not -take advantage of this magnificent opportunity lo show the world what we have done with our resources as well as what they are going to do to bring Canada into the forefront of the nations before the end of this, our special century.
Boards of Trade and other public bodies have been consulted and in every case a favourable answer has been received. I wish to quote a few lines from letters written by the mayors of several cities and towns of Canada. The mayor of Prince Rupert:
I am sure that the city of Prince Rupert, and district tributary, would be glad to do their share towards making the exposition a success.
The mayor of Quebec:
As Mayor of Quebec, the oldest of our cities, the cradle of the nation, I would contemplate with pleasure, together with all the Quebeckers, the success of a Canadian Universal Exhibition, to celebrate the fiftieth anniversary of the Confederation of the provinces.
The time seems to be well chosen, at the first period of the twentieth century, who should be Canada's century, if one takes into consideration the very rapid and extensive progress of our country.
The mayor of Welland:
To reply to your favour of the 13th insi., I wish to say that I heartily endorse the idea to celebrate the fiftieth birthday of our Dominion. It seems to me that all Canadians should jump at the opportunity presented at that time to do something really large, to advertise Canada and draw the attention of the whole civilized world to the wonderful progress we have made in the fifty years of Confederation.
The mayor of Campbellton, N.B.:
In reply to your esteemed favour of the 11th inst., regarding the holding of an Inter-Imperial Exposition in Canada during the year 1917 or 1918, I certainly think the project is one which will commend itself to all citizens of this Dominion, as it will prove, if properly handled, of incalculable benefit. I had the pleasure of attending the Toronto exhibition this year and I feel sure that if the proposed exhibition were carried out along the lines pursued by the

managers of the Toronto exhibition, it would prove an unqualified success.
The mayor of Chatham:
Pardon one suggestion, viz: in the event of a decision in favour of holding the exposition, I would propose it be laid before the official board that a publicity officer be appointed in every city and town of importance in Canada, to zealously strive for the success of the project. Mayor Hocken, Toronto:
It is needless to say that I heartily agree that the jubilee of Canadian Confederation is an event worthy of being celebrated in some appropriate manner.
