The mayor of Windsor:
1 am in receipt of your letter of the 11th. The project of holding a Universal Exhibition in Canada in the near future, to celebrate the fiftieth anniversary of the birth of our Dominion, is one which must commend itself to every citizen of Canada, and indeed to all the British Empire. The time has long since passed when anyone professing a degree of reading, experience or judgment, can doubt that the dayspring is at hand, and that we are on the eve of a world-wide transformation wherein Canada must perforce play a leading part, but in which her just dues shall be accorded to her only by the exercise of that measure of effort on the part of her people, which is at all times the price of success.
The mayor of Cobalt:
I consider it would be a great mistake if such an occasion should be allowed to pass without a monster exhibit of the forward strides which our Dominion has made in the first fifty years of its existence and of the wonderful advancement of our institutions and our industries.
The mayor of Belleville:
Would not this be a time at which our King could attend	and open this	great	nationalgathering of	the	empire?	It	may	appear a
little ambitious on the part of Canada, but it would illustrate to the world that the empire is a real living power.
The mayor of	Calgary:
On behalf	of	Calgary	in	particular and!
Southern Alberta in general, I can promise you every support that can be given you in your endeavours to make known to the world the fact that the Dominion of Canada has now grown to be one of the most valuable assets of the British empire.
The mayor of Calgary adds:
I suggest that you call the attention of your association to the fact that Calgary is' the most ideal Convention city in Canada, and also one of the most progressive and prosperous

cities in America and well worthy of consideration as a place of meeting for Canada's universal exhibition celebration.
The mayor of Hamilton.
I consider that an exposition of this character would bring Canada before the attention of the nations of the world in a manner that would prove to be a revelation to them of the immensity of our Dominion, its vast resources, and its many great manufacturing and commercial enterprises, which would no doubt result in lasting good to this country.
He adds:
I confess to a little disappointment in not seeing Hamilton ' the Birmingham of Canada ' mentioned in the list of cities contained in the special cable to the correspondent of the Montreal Star. I will, however, be greatly pleased to further the project to the best of my ability.
The mayor of Port Arthur:
This letter was read before council last night, and one and all are in thorough sympathy and accord with the movement, and will do their share to enthuse the citizens here.
I have about 1,000 similar letters, written from all parts of Canada. The letters sent by the various municipal councils and public bodies all favour the idea of the commemoration, by way of an international exposition, of the fiftieth anniversary of the Confederation. But I must be frank; several of the correspondents are inclined to favour their own cities and towns, which is, after all, quite legitimate. I admit that every one has a right to be proud of his own city or town, but the main thing is that all agree as to the chief proposal. My resolution does not favour one city or the other, but were I asked what my sentiment is, I would say that Montreal, the commercial metropolis, is the place for such an exposition. However, the choice will rest with the Government. The last words of Lord Strathcona, justly called the great empire builder, spoken in his London office to a correspondent of La Presse, were in favour of the holding of a universal exposition on the occasion of the fiftieth anniversary of that Confederation, in which he played such a prominent part.
And why should we hold such an exposition? I contend that it would be highly educational and at the same time it would possess great commercial advantages for this country. I shall read an extract from a lecture delivered by Mr. De Bray, an authority in such matters. He is the principal of L'Ecole des Hautes Etudes Com-merciales of Montreal. On Friday, the 6th of March last, he delivered a lecture, in the course of which he said:
The creation of national exhibitions is greatly facilitated by the universal or international exhibitions, because the large grounds which have to be reserved for a universal exhibition admirably serve, henceforth, the purpose of the national exhibition. And that is why, in London, we have now the Crystal Palace, in Brussels the 'Halls du Cinquantenaire,' and in Paris the Trocadero which are now permanent institutions and in the same time remain as admirable souvenirs of the great exhibitions of the past.
As regards the commercial point of view, the great exhibitions always produce an extraordinary recrudescence of commercial activities, through the enormous influx of foreign capital, which has a tendency to stay, even long after the gates of the exhibition have been closed. And then there is also the great impetus given to the railways, which have to carry the many thousands of sight seers. It is also a well established fact that, during an international exhibition, the operations of the clearing ing house have been far more important than at other times, and the explanation resides in the fact that all branches of trade are then taxed to their utmost, through the presence of so mdny large crowds, whose wants have got to be perforce attended to. We have a proof of that in the fact that during the last exhibition of 1900 in Paris, there were deposited in the savings banks over three hundred millions dollars more than in former years.
But the advantages to be derived from an international exhibition must not be calculated only from a mercenary point of view, and indeed the moral aspect also possesses a very appreciable value. We must not lose sight that the thousands and thousands of foreign Visitors must henceforth serve admirably the purpose of putting our country in a better light in the eyes of the world, if only we can teach them in the right way the lesson which I am sure we are well able to give them. And the natural sequence of all that is that there are closer diplomatic relations between nations which have now learned to appreciate one another. And then, also, what about the great influence on the masses of the people, during exhibition time, through the gorgeous pageants at certain fixed intervals, the great labour celebrations and allegorical representations, the inauguration of monuments, etc.
As regards the educational side of the question, what better lessons could we wish for the pupils of our schools than the knowledge imparted by the sight of the innumerable marvels of a great exhibition. All trades and professions are here specially interested, and more particularly those that are of a technical kind, as the student sees there, so to say at a glance, all the great inventions and all the methods of modern fabrication which are the wonder of the age, and constitute the indispensable complement of technical education.
Sir, all countries, great and small, old and new, have had, and will have in the future, their world's fairs. As Canadians, we have taken part in nearly all the universal expositions which have been held for the last forty years, and with great profit to Canada.
In conclusion, Sir, we must commemorate the fiftieth anniversary of Confederation. Our constitution is the best evidence of

British statesmanship; it is based fundamentally on law, order, justice and freedom. Political economists agree that it is because of those strong features in British institutions generally that our empire endures.
The dedication, in 1908, of the plains of Abraham on the occasion of the tercenten-nary of Quebec was the solemn homage of a united people to the valour and heroism of both the victor and the vanquished. The commemoration of the semi-centennial of Confederation will mark our appreciation of tfte happy development of British institutions in North America. It is in that spirit and in that spirit alone that I now hare the honour to move the resolution *which stands in my name. One event, the dedication of the plains of Abraham in 1908, was the expression of our admiration of 'j glorious past; let the other, the commemoration of the serm-centennial of our Confederation, be for every Canadian the expression of our high hopes for the brilliant future that awaits this, our great country.

My hon.
friend, in proposing this motion, has presented to the House a very admirable, interesting and comprehensive review of the growth and development of constitutional self-government in His Majesty's Dominions of North America. In the course of his remarks he has commenced from the very beginning; he has taken us back to 1774 and has traced the progress of autonomous self-government from that time up to the 1st day of July, 1867, when the foundations of the present Dominion were laid.
It is beyond question-on this I think there will be no division of opinion in this House or indeed in the country-that when we reach the fiftieth anniversary. of that date, that great anniversary should be worthily commemorated in this country. I have not the slightest doubt that other portions of the empire would be desirous of joining us in celebrating that event, which was an event not full of significance for this Dominion alone, as then constituted or as now constituted, but was an event fraught with great significance for the future growth and development, influence and destiny of the whole empire. Therefore, so far as the observations of my hon. friend commend to the attention of tne House, of the Government and of the people of the country a worthy celebration of the event, there should, it seems to me, be nc division of opinion on that "object.

My hon. friend, however, devoted particular attention to the consideration of a projected international exhibition on that occasion. He has placed before us information of perhaps not a very definite character as to what is proposed, and-he has shown us that the project which he has in mind has support not only in this country but in the British Isles as well and that support has been given by various representative bodies. The subject is one which must engage the attention of Parliament and of the Government in the early future, because, if there is to be a worthy and suitable commemoration of the anniversary alluded to, it is perfectly obvious that the preparation for that celebration cannot be delayed until the last moment. I do not at the moment dissent from the view, although I have given to it very little consideration and have an entirely open mind on the subject, that an international or a great exhibition of some kind might very properly be held on that occasion and as part of the celebration. It seems to me, however, that we have not before us at the present time such information, as to precisely what is proposed or as to the means or methods by which it could be carried out, as would justify the House in giving an expression of opinion on the subject to-day. I am in entire sympathy with the observations of my hon. friend the member for Rouville so far as the object which he desires to obtain is concerned in itself, .but I would suggest to him that, until we have information of a somewhat more precise character as to what is proposed, it would be well for us not to commit ourselves too distinctly to any definite or specific project. If Parliament should be of opinion that a great exhibition, whether international or otherwise, should form a necessary or desirable part of the celebration which my hon. friend has discussed and advocated, it might well be that such an exhibition ought to be taken in hand by the Government itself, with the sanction and approval of Parliament, and that all the various bodies which have commended the project should be invited to lend their aid and assistance for the purpose of making that exhibition a great success. Until, however, we can come more definitely to a conclusion, after the fullest consideration as to what ought to be done in that regard, whether by the Government or by some representative body outside of the Government, it would perhaps be undesirable and unnecessary that we should commit ourselves to the pro-

posal embodied in this resolution. I would be inclined therefore to move the adjournment of the debate in order to afford to the House fuller opportunity of considering what is proposed and of understanding it more clearly, because, while the speech of my hon. friend was very admirable as regards the growth and development of constitutional self-government in this country, only a small part of his speech was devoted to placing before the House the exact proposal which he has in mind. At the moment I shall not move the adjournment of the House, as there may be hon. gentlemen on either side of the House desirous of giving their ideas and suggestions as to what my hon. friend from Rouville has proposed. In so far as he proposes a worthy celebration of the great anniversary alluded to, I am entirely in sympathy with what he has said.

I am sure we have all listened with a great deal of satisfaction to the remarks of the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux). His speech was very interesting, and it will commend itself to the people of Canada that this occasion should be worthily celebrated by this country. I wish to bring to the attention of the House the fact that the province of Prince Edward Island is about to celebrate, in August next, the first conference of Confederation. You are aware, Sir, that from the year 1854, the time at which the Confederation of the province was mooted in the Parliament of the province of Nova Scotia, up to 1864, no meeting of the representatives of the provinces was held to bring about the consummation of this idea, though the idea was prevalent not only amongst the poeple of the provinces but amongst the people of the old country as well. A resolution was passed in the legislature of Nova Scotia in 1862, which appears in a book issued by Hon. Edward Whelan, who was the secretary of tihe first conference of Confederation held in the city of Charlottetown. That resolution reads as follows:
Whereas the subject of a union of the North American provinces, or of the Maritime provinces of British America, has been from time to time mooted and discussed in all the colonies ;
And whereas while many advantages may be secured from such a union either of ail these provinces, or of a portion of them, many and serious obstacles are presented which can only be overcome by mutual consultation of the leading men of the colonies, and by free communication with the Imperial Government; therefore Resolved, that His Excellency the
Lieutenant Governor be respectfully requested to put himself in communication with His Grace the Colonial Secretary, and His Excellency the Governor General, and the Lieutenant Governors of the North American provinces, in order to ascertain the policy of her Majesty's Government and the opinions of the other colonies, with a view to an enlightened consideration of a question involving the highest interest, and upon which the public mind in all the provinces ought to be set at rest.
A copy of this resolution was sent to the Duke of Newcastle, who was then Colonial Secretary, and he, on the 6th of July, 1862, sent the resolution to the different colonies. He did not express on behalf of the British Government any opinion as to the advisability of this union, but it was well known at the time from the expressions of opinion in the British Parliament that the people of Great Britain were very anxious that the union of the colonies should take place. In pursuance of this resolution, other resolutions were passed in 1864 in the legislatures of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. The resolution passed in the legislature of Prince Edward Island reads as follows:
Resolved, that His Excellency the Lieutenant Governor be authorized to appoint delegates (not to exceed five), to confer with delegates who may be appointed by the Governments of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick for the purpose of discussing the expediency of a Union of the three provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island under one Government and Legislature, the report of the said delegates to be laid before the Legislature of this colony, before any further action shall be taken in regard to the proposed question.
-A similar resolution was passed in the legislatures of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, and a conference was arranged to take place in the city of Charlottetown, in Prince Edward Island, in the month of September, 1864. So soon as it became mooted that this conference for the consolidation of the three Maritime provinces was to take place, the legislatures and representative men of the provinces of Upper and Lower Canada tasked to be permitted to join in the conference. The premiers and members of the governments of the Upper provinces came to Charlottetown and entered into conference with the representatives from the three Maritime provinces. It was found that it was not thought advisable to consolidate the three Maritime provinces, and the consensus of opinion which was held in the conference was that all the British American colonies should be consolidated in one confederation. Nothing definite took place in that

conference at Charlottetown, except the expression of that opinion. It was agreed that another conference should be held and the confederation enacted into law. Speeches were made at that conference by Sir George Etienne Cartier, Sir John A. Macdonald and other eminent men. It was decided that these leaders should tour the Maritime provinces and also the Upper provinces, and that the final conference on Confederation should take place in the city of Quebec. They entered upon this tour, and at each of the different capitals they were royally entertained. They came to the city of Quebec, and on the 10th of October, 1864, the agreement of Confederation was drawn up and consented to by the delegates from all the provinces with the exception of those from the province of Prince Edward Island, who did not see their way to agree to the terms set forth in the report of the conference.
Now, I consider that although the final consummation of this conference took place in 1867, some consideration should be given to the first conference of Confederation which took place in the city of Charlottetown in 1864. The people of Prince Edward Island would be glad to see every member of the House of Commons join the assembly in the city of Charlottetown to commemorate this great event, the greatest and most momentous event in the history of our country. The city of Charlottetown is the cradle of Confederation. All the delegates who afterwards were at Quebec assembled in the city of Charlottetown, and the opinions formed in the Charlottetown conference were the opinions which were afterwards enacted into law and became the British North America Act. Now, while I am not opposed to having the Confederation event, the great event of the consolidation as finally accomplished, celebrated as suggested by the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux), I think some consideration should be given by the Parliament to the celebration to take place in the city of Charlottetown in the month of August next. I bring this to your consideration because it may not be generally known that the Island Province has taken upon itself to celebrate in a proper manner the great event in our history, and I think it is due to Prince Edward Island that this Parliament should give consideration to the celebration of Confederation in the place of its nativity. I would ask that when this matter comes up, if the Government does bring it up, my suggestion should receive the unanimous support of

the members of this House, as I know' it will receive the approval of every man in Canada who approves the Confederation of these provinces. At the time of Confederation our population was only three millions; to-day we have a population of eight or nine millions, with a prospect in a few years of having a population of over thirty millions. Here is an event, the consolidation of our country, the celebration of which should receive the favourable attention of this Parliament. And, although the final consummation of the Confederation project will receive greater consideration than the event of which I have spoken, still this momentous conference in the city of Charlottetown should receive great consideration at the hands of this House and the country.

The matter which the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemiuex) has brought to the attention of the House is certainly deserving of careful consideration. It goes witn-out saying that the fiftieth anniversary of the Confederation of the Canadian provinces should be celebrated in some fitting manner, and the hon. member for Eouville deserves the thanks of the House for having brought the matter to our attention. His further suggestion, however, that the celebration should take the form of an international exhibition, is a matter that will require very careful consideration. In the remarks of my hon. friend in this rega-d I did not detect quite as much enthusiasm as I have observed in his remarks upon subjects of lesser importance on previous occasions. I do not suppose we are justified in saying that this was because of a lack of sympathy, but he certainly did not express himself as emphatically upon the idea of an international exhibition as I think he should do if he 'believes that that is the best way of celebrating the fiftieth anniversary of Canadian Confederation.

The main object of my resolution is to commemorate the semi-centennial of the Canadian Confederation. It is suggested that it should be commemorated by an international or universal exposition; of course, I await the judgment of the Government on that point.

I quite understand
the position of the hon. gentleman. I would point out, however, that, in respect of cost the matter of an international exposition is one of very serious importance. Having regard to the international exhibitions that have been held on this continent during

the last thirty or forty years, what is the financial experience of the cities in which they have been held and of the communities that have had to pay for them? I think the hon. member for Rouville will agree that if an international exhibition is to be held, it must be a good one, and one worthy of this country. Look at the history of the exhibition that was held at Chicago, in connection with which I believe, millions of dollars were sunk, never to be recovered. The experience .of Buffalo was very similar, and the same may toe said of St. Louis and other cities in which such exhibitions have been held. It is hardly to be expected that the Dominion of Canada could make a paying enterprise out of an international exhibition. In the first place, the Government would have to come down with a good round sum-I hesitate to name the amount without further consideration, but it would have to be a large sum. Further, a contribution from the Dominion Government would not be sufficient to make such an exhibition successful; it would have to be backed up by the people of Canada; the producers of Canada in all lines-in the mines, the farms and the forests-who send exhibits on such occasions would all have to make some personal sacrifice in order to make such an exhibition the success it should be.
It is hardly necessary that I should enter into all the details to which my hon. friend referred with regard to the location of such an exhibition, but that would also be a very important matter, and one that would have a great deal to do with the success of the project. The hon. gentleman read several letters showing that certain cities throughout the Dominion of Canada were ready and willing to accept the responsibility of holding the fair. But it must be borne in mind that any city in which such an exhibition is held must have more hotel accommodation than many of these cities have. It would have to be a large city; I do not know whether the hon. member for Queens, Prince Edward Island (Mr. McLean), has one big enough or not; I am a little doubtful whether he has, but, in any case, there are only four or five cities in the Dominion of Canada that could furnish anything like the accommodation that would be required if the public of all nations were invited. It is evident to everyone that the hotel accommodation in such a centre would have to be the very best. In that respect I think the city of Toronto has more to commend it than any other city. It would take a fairly good international exhibition to beat the one that is held in Toronto every year, and surely,
if the Dominion of Canada is to go into the exhibition business, it must do something which will exceed the results which are accomplished by any one city. The exhibition which is held at Toronto is looked upon as one of the very finest annual exhibitions in the whole world. I have travelled a good deal, and I am sure that there is not in the whole world an annual exhibition that equals the one held in the city of Toronto every year. I do not know whether the hon. member for Rouville has considered a celebration of any other nature which would be equally as good, perhaps less expensive and less liable to failure, than the one that he suggests. I quite agree with him that it is absolutely necessary that some kind of celebration should be held, but whether we are prepared to commit ourselves at the first blush to so large a project is a matter for consideration.
I have referred to the financial aspect of the matter, and to the location, which should be central. Another respect in which the province of Ontario has advantages in this regard is that it has the goods to show, so far as Canadian products are concerned. More than half the industrial products and forty per cent of the agricultural products of Canada are produced in that pro vince, so that we have a large supply of goods near at hand if the city of Toronto or some other central point be selected. Then, the transportation facilities would be a very important factor. The city of Toronto has a good harbour in the summer time; the lake travel is very pleasant, the people can be brought from the East and from the West not only by our railways but by handsome steamers that ply- at intervals across the lakes and up and down the river St. Lawrence. Those who visit Canada for the first time would have an opportunity of seeing some of the most magnificent scenery the world can afford. Unfortunately we in Canada who are born almost within the sound of Niagara Falls do not regard them with very much wonder; possibly, like the Irishman, our only wonder is that the waters do not fall up instead of down. In any case, we live so close to them that we do not appreciate their wonderful beauty. Niagara Falls can be reached from Toronto within two hours; you have also lake Ontario, the beautiful river St. Lawrence, the Muskoka lakes, and other points within one hundred or one hundred and fifty miles of the city-points of interest that cannot be rivalled, perhaps, in any other part of Canada.

Then to have the stuff to feed the people with is an important consideration. The high cost of living is increased when you place a large number of people in a city hr town that is incapable, in an ordinary way, of looking after their requirements. The city of Toronto is placed in the heart of a great agricultural district that could supply all the wants of all the poeple who would visit that city on such an occasion, without unduly raising the rates in the hotels. I think the idea which the hon. gentleman has advanced is a good one, but I feel that the exhibition part of it must be considered very carefully. If the Government decides to take up this celebration it must be well supported. Whatever is done must be done well. To attempt a great project of this nature half heartedly, or in such a way as not to make a success of it, is something that we cannot contemplate. We are all optimists in this respect, that whatever we take hold of we believe we are able to do and are prepared to do well. Therefore I approve the suggestion made by the right hon. leader of the House that it would be well if my hon. friend would consent to have the debate adjourned until further consideration can be given to the question; and, if it is in order, I would move now that the debate be adjourned.

I have listened to the debate, and it does not altogether commend itself to me. My view is that if this experiment of Confederation is to be celebrated at the end of its fiftieth year, that celebration should take the practical form of a revision of our Constitution. It is an old constitution now in many respects, and ought to be revised. For instance, our Parliamentary procedure needs revision. For fifteen years we have been passing laws for the Dominion of Canada and we have not yet found a way of enforcing federal laws. That is an important question. We are talking of a celebration; I would like to see the fiftieth anniversary of Confederation, if it has proved a success, celebrated by a revision of the Constitution, in the direction of its improvement and simplification.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I wish to draw to your attention some important facts in connection with this case, which, in my judgment deserve more than a passing notice and which I think should be brought to the attention of this House, and through this House to the attention of this country. A great wrong has been done by somebody. A large amount of money has been taken from the public treasury which ought not to have been taken. I know not whether it be the fault of the Department of Railways and Canals as a department, or whether it be the fault of one of its officials or whether it be the fault of a combination of officials. I only know that a great wrong has been done, and if I accomplish nothing else than to make the matter plain before the House and the country, I shall feel that I have not spent my time in vain.
I learned of the existence of this condition of affairs through a lawsuit which was carried on in the courts of the province of New Brunswick in the month of January last. The case was tried in the city of Fredericton, the capital of the province, and lasted, 1 think, eleven or twelve days. ' The action was brought by a man named John E. Stewart against the Southampton Railway Company to recover damages resulting from the breach of an agreement. The agreement, dated the 10th of September, 1910, w'as between John E. Stewart, a landowner of the county of Victoria, of the first part, and the Southampton Railway Company, of the second part. The Southampton Railway Company agreed to assign, and did assign so far as they were able to do so, all bonds which thereafter might be guaranteed by the legislature of New Brunswick and all subsidies which they might obtain from the Parliament of Canada, entirely without condition simply to build the railroad according to the provisions that might be required by the legislature of New Brunswick in an Act thereafter to be passed guaranteeing the bonds.	The contract
remained in force for something like two and a half months, when the directors of

the company were called together. By a formal resolution they rescinded the contract and took it away from the contractor in as ample a manner as they possibly could. In the meantime the contractor had commenced operations, had spent some money, let a sub-contract to a man by the name of Claude McDonald-
Order.

It is not the original Claude Macdonell. The original Claude does not go into small things like this. Some differences arose between the company and the contractor. The company claimed that Stewart had obtained his contract by making fraudulent representations as to his financial ability. With that branch of the case I do not intend to deal, unless some hon. gentleman is curious enough to delve into it; that branch plays no part here. The question I want to discuss is whether or not the Dominion of Canada has been unfairly treated-I might almost go so far as to say robbed-by the machinations of this railway company and its friends. When the contract was taken away from Stewart he brought an action against the company for damages, the measure of damages claimed being the difference between the sum received by the company in the way of bonds and subsidies, and the amount for which the road could have been constructed by him according to the plans and specifications and conditions of this contract. While no plans and specifications were mentioned in the contract, specifications had been made by Stewart himself and an engineer in his employ and were in existence at the time the contract was signed. The road, according to his evidence, was to be built, and was built, according to those plans and specifications, the only difference being that the specifications had 'been modified to some extent in two or three places in order to reduce the cost of construction. Stewart contended that he could have made a large profit in building this road for the bonds and subsidies had he been allowed to do so under his original contract. The contract having been taken away from him, the action for damages was brought. The matter was delayed by the defendant just as long as it was possible. The writ was issued in the month of September, 1912. We did not get down to trial until January, 1914, because every device known to counsel was resorted to by counsel for the defence to prevent this matter coming to trial. Finally when all the technical and legal cobwebs were
brushed away, we got squared away in Fredericton in January last.
To show what rights this company had in this Parliament, I just wish to cite from Chapter 48 of the Statutes of Canada, 1912, that is, the Railway Subsidies Act. The Southampton Railway Company was included in that Act for a general subsidy not to exceed thirteen miles. Subsection 23 of section 2 reads:
To the Southampton Railway Company, for a line of railway from a point at or near Millville to a point on the St. John river near the Pikiok Bridge, not exceeding 13 miles.
And the general provisions of the Railway Subsidies Act provided that the Governor in Council might pay to any of these companies building a road which did not cost more than $15,000 a mile, the sum of $3,200 a mile as a subsidy; and for every $1,000 expended on the road per mile above the $15,000, $500 could be paid in the way of a subsidy. Figured out, that meant that when the road reached over a cost of $21,400 a mile, the double subsidy of $6,400 was available. I only mention this fact to make the argument plain.
In the 1911 session of the New Brunswick Legislature, as the Minister of Marine will remember, legislation was passed authorizing the Lieutenant-Governor-in-Council to guarantee the bonds of this company to the extent of $10,000 per mile, and, in its 1912 session, this Parliament included the Southampton Railway Company under the general subsidy for a road costing $15,000 per mile. This company then had available the four per cent guaranteed bonds, principal and interest, of the province of New Brunswick, for $10,000 per mile, and they had a single subsidy of $3,200 per mile from this Parliament, making in all $13,200 per mile. Up to that time, it was never dreamed by any person that this road would cost anything more than $15,000 per mile, because all the men in the company put together, with the exception of one who was simply filling in as a member of the family, could not raise enough to buiid one mile of road. It was one of the most complete family compacts you ever heard of. It consisted first of Mr. James K. Pinder, a very prominent member of the Legislature of New Brunswick, a man who always has been, and always will be, I presume, a warm supporter of the Minister of Marine," and I am sure he will be proud to acknowledge him as such; Mr. John A. Stewart, the plaintiff in the suit, who was vice-president; James K. Pinder's son, George Pinder; Dr. McNully, who was James K. Pinder's son-in-law; Mr. Gilman,

an estimable old gentleman, 74 years old, whose daughter was the wife of George Pinder. So you see it was a complete family compact, outside of my client, the plaintiff. Stewart was the first president and managing director. After they quarrelled with him, he was relieved of the position, and Mr. Pinder was made president, but after a time I think he was relieved of the position and his son-in-law. Dr. McNully, was made president. I should have mentioned that there was another, a Mr. Guthrie, a legal gentleman of Fredericton, who is now a member of the New Brunswick Legislature, and who acted as the legal adviser and secretary of the company.
This contract was 'made before they had received the guarantee of bonds or the subsidy from this Parliament, but they had in their possession an Order in Council, passed by the Executive Council of New Brunswick in the month of March or April, 1910, agreeing to guarantee the bonds to the extent of $10,000 per mile under certain conditions, and that the Government would ask the necessary authority at the next session of the legislature to guarantee the bonds. They were attempting to build the road and finance it on this Order in Council. The road was to be between 12 and 13 miles, running from the Millville branch line of the Canadian Pacific railway in the county of York to the River St. John. I admit frankly that when the road was first thought of; when the scheme first originated in the brain of Mr. Pinder, while it was not perhaps a very good proposition, it was a great necessity at that time for the people of that part of New Brunswick.
I would have found no fault if the Minister of Marine had guaranteed the bonds of that road in 1909, because everything seemed clear; it was a feasible proposition and would have been at least a good fair business move. But in the year 1910 things had begun to change. A great agitation had started in New Brunswick to construct a road down the St. John river, popularly known as the St. John Valley railway. There is a distance between Woodstock and Fredericton of about 62 miles along the St. John river, which has been inhabited for over a hundred years, and it may seem remarkable that it has been left absolutely without railway communication. They have this branch of the Canadian Pacific railway about 13 miles away to the east, and they had another branch of the Canadian Pacific railway to the west, a little greater distance away, but there was this beauti-[ Mr. Carvell. ]
ful river valley without any railway communication. The idea at the beginning was that this branch road should tap the river St. John where it was crossed by a splendid highway bridge, pretty nearly in the centre between Woodstock and Fredericton, and in that way, that it would draw traffic both north and south, up and down the river, and that probably, with the local traffic along the line, there would be sufficient traffic to fairly well support the road. An agreement was afterwards made by which this road, when constructed, was to be operated by the Canadian Pacific railway and as a matter of fact the road is now being operated by that company, the Canadian Pacific railway paying to the province 40 per cent of the gross earnings with which to satisfy the interest on the bonds, and the balance, if any, is to go to the company. I am afraid it will be a long time before the company realizes anything over and above the amount necessary to pay the bond issue.
It was sworn at the trial that they were determined to start this road without the bonds, and without the subsidy, and without legislation of any kind, in order that it might be a means of checking the construction of the line down the river. Happily it turned out that their schemes were not well laid, and they were not able to defeat the greater project. I do say here, that in view of the fact that the greater project had to go on, it was poor policy, it was no business policy at all, it was practically squandering the amount of money for which the province of New Brunswick guaranteed these bonds, to guarantee them at all. I know the Minister of Marine may take issue with me on that, but I tried to make it plain that had the larger scheme not gone on, had the Valley laihvay not been built, then I would look upon this railway not only as a good business scheme, but a real necessity to give that portion of the province railway communication. It is only thirteen miles from the railway to the river; there is a branch of the Canadian Pacific railway on one side, and they have the Valley railway, which will be operated by the Intercolonial railway on the other, and no person would have to travel more than six or seven miles, in any portion of that territory, to get to a railway. It is a country not very well settled; it is not in a very high state of agricultural development; it is just the medium ordinary land we have in the Maritime provinces. I should mention that halfway between these two points, this Mr. Pinder, the politician of the whole scheme,

had a little sawmill, whose product might be 500,000 a year, and I doubt il it ever exceeded one million. He therefore would only have six miles to draw his lumber to the railway. The bonds were guaranteed later on, and after that, this Parliament granted the subsidy, which really is the matter I am now discussing.
I feel it incumbent on me to give a somewhat historical description of the railway, in order that the House may fully understand the true situation. The railway company, after they cancelled the contract with Stewart, made a contract with Mr. Binder, in which, as it appeared from the evidence, Mr. Pimder was given exactly the same rights and conditions as Stewart had been given in the former contract. Pinder was given all the bonds 'and all the subsidies, and was to build a road the specifications of which, as I understand it, were left entirely blank. Pander carried on the work which Stewart had commenced, and in the fall of 1911 the company let a contract to the firm of Wm. McDonald and Son, of Fredericton, who built the first section of tlhe road, which is six miles from Millville, on the Canadian Pacific line, to Binder's mill. The next contract was let in March, 1912, and they worked until some time in October, when the work was practically completed.
In looking around to find out what this road had cost, because that was the measure of our damages, I naturally thought that the proper person to look to was the man w(ho had built the road. Therefore I subpoenaed Messrs. McDonald and Son as my principal witnesses. A man by the name of Claude McDonald, with whom Stewart had 'entered into a contract, was continued, and did a certain amount of the work; I therefore subpoenaed him. Having subpoenaed Claude McDonald and William McDonald and Son, I thought that I had the men who had built the road.
Built six miles of the road.

The whole of it. Claude McDonald had a subcontract on the first six miles. Messrs. Wm. McDonald and Son, on their first contract, completed that six-mile contract, and on their second contract completed the road. I have the evidence of these gentlemen in the report of the stenographer of the court. Under the contract they were to do everything with regard to the road -except ito furnish rails, sleepers, bridges and right of way,
which, of course, were furnished by the company.
By every means in my power, I tried to find out from the company themselves what the road had cost; but this is the position in which I found myself. The company had contracted with Pinder to build the road, and Pinder was the company and the company was Pinder. They had given all the bonds and all the subsidies to Pinder. When I subpoenaed the company to produce their books and papers, they said that they did not have any. When I subpoenaed the company to produce their plans and profiles, they said that they did not have any. When I asked them to tell me what the road and bridges cost, they said that they did not know. When I asked them as to the cost of the rails and the sleepers, they said:	'We did not buy any; we handed
everything over to Mr. Pinder, and Mr. Pinder was the man who did all the buying.' When I put Mr. Pinder on the stand and asked him the question, he said:	'I do
not know; I have not any books and I have not any papers.' Mr. Pinder refused to tell anything. He simply said ' I do not know.' Therefore I was compelled to get the best evidence that I could elsewhere. I am going to give some of the evidence which I obtained, because in order that the Department of Railways and Canals would be warranted in paying this subsidy, this road must have cost $21,400 a mile on an average. If it had cost $15,000 a mile on an average, the department would have been justified in paying a subsidy of $3,200. For every thousand dollars a mile of cost above that, the department would have paid $500. Therefore I called as the first important witness a Mr. W. Henry Maxwell. Before I go into that, I think I had better read to the House a report made to the department by its officer, because it is upon this report, I understand, that the money was paid; it is this report which I am attacking, and.it is the people who are responsible for this report, whoever they may be, that I am trying to ferret out. Therefore, I think that we should have this report on ' Hansard.' My hon. friend the acting Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Reid) was kind enough to send this to me when I wrote him as he knew that I would subpoena an officer of the department. It answered my purpose just as well as an officer of the department would have done. Therefore I have that part of the return already. The covering letter of this report is as follows:

Department of Railways and Canals.
Office of the Inspecting Engineer.
Ottawa, 4th November, 1913. W. A. Bowden, Esq.,
Chief Engineer,
Department of Railways and Canals.
Sir,
On the 23rd, ultimo, I inspected, on subsidy account the Southampton railway, accompanied by Mr. Pinder, M.L.A., President, and beg to report.
The line starts at a point on the Canadian Pacific railway, near Millville, N.B., and runs in a southerly direction to a point on the St. John river near Pokiok bridge, the length being 12.7 miles.
My report of October 14, 1912 contains a description of the various features of the line.
Since last report the following work has been done.
The banks have been widened and lifted where required and the road bed put in good shape.
Track is laid throughout with 56 lb. rails from the Fredericton branch of the Canadian Pacific railway. The rails are in good serviceable condition, equal in every respect to those in use on the Gibson branch.
Ballasting has been completed throughout to the full depth required by the contract.
The two steel bridges have been erected and all structures are completed.
A water tank of 10,000 gals, capacity has been erected at the south end, with gravity supply, there are also at the south end a neat station building, engine house, and turntable. A similar station building is erected at Pinder mile 7.
Herewith is a statement of the cost of the road amounting to $291,517 or $22,954 per mile.
I have to report the line as completed in accordance with the contract dated 14th May, 1912.
I have the honour to be,
Sir,
Your obedient servant,
(Sgd) E. V. Johnson,
Inspecting Engineer.
Subsidy Statement.
The line is subsidized by Act of 1912, Chap. 48 for a distance not exceeding 13 miles. The actual length is 12.7 miles.
12-7 miles at $6,400 per mile = $81,200.
This road will be operated by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company.

Now, I have taken some time to put that on ' Hansard,1' but I had to do so in order to discuss this matter intelligently. I make the statement here to-night, and we have the proof in incontestable evidence, evidence that they did not attempt to rebut or refute, that the road did not cost $12,500 a mile. I am satisfied that the figures I am going to give as to its cost are above the actual amount in many respects. I gave the evidence so far as I could get it, but on a few of the items I had to take the estimates of engineers and practical men. On these figures, even with the most liberal allowance, we could not figure the cost of the road at above $12,000 a mile. Yet the engineer of the Department of Railways and Canals certified that the railway cost $22,954 a mile-practically $23,000-a mile. I tried to call the engineer who had charge of the road, but unfortunately the man got very ill the day the subpoena was served upon him and remained very, very ill until I .sent word by nis doctor that if he would come out and give evidence I would not ask him any questions about this report. Then the man got able to come to court. But when he got to court, he did not know anything about what anything cost on tne whole road; he had no books, no papers, no plans, no profiles, no specifications. , He did not even know how much money he had got from the contractor or how much he was going to get. He only knew that he was the engineer on tne work. But I was able to get one very valuable piece of evidence from him. I have here the estimates which he gave the contractors, William McDonald & Son, down to the 1st of October, 1912, and that was practically the end of the McDonalds' work. I have not the original here. I may explain, tnat there was a little legal difficulty between William McDonald & Son and Mr. Pinder. McDonald & Son. were suing Pinder, and the matter wa3 to be tried at the January sitting of the York Circuit, but I understand the case was settled amicably out of court. When I left Fredericton, I was not able to bring the original estimate because it was needed by Messrs. McDonald in the suit they were pressing. But I have a copy here whicn I think hon. gentlemen will accept as correct. It is made by myself, and is a verbatim copy of the estimates made by the engineer. And I did get the engineer to admit that it was his, which he could hardly have avoided admitting because every word and every figure of the original was in his handwriting.

What is the name of the
engineer?

Mr. David W. Brown.
Now I wish to read this and place it alongside the other in order that-
That is Pinder's engineer.

Yes, that is what he
said. There was no company's engineer, because the company had handed over everything it had to Mr. Pinder. Mr. Pinder was, to all intents and purposes, the company. I had great difficulty in getting the document in as evidence. I produced the document from Mr. William McDonald, but objection was taken on the ground that any evidence given by David Brown to Mr. McDonald against Mr. Pinder was not evidence as against the company because Mr. Pinder was not the company. But after I got Mr. Brown into court, I was able to get the evidence in. The work was in two sections, the first from Millville to Mr. Pinder's mill, and second from Mr. Pinder's mill to the river. How much work did the hon.
gentleman say was done in solid rock?

In the first contract,
1,398 yards; in the second contract, 2,825 yards, a total oE 4,423 cubic yards.

Is that all the rock work
that was done?

That is all the rock
work that was done. I know my hon. friend is surprised that in the building of thirteen miles of road only 4,400 cubic yards of solid rock should be removed. But when my hon. friend remembers that this road simply followed the surface; that they .used seven degree curves when necessary; that only enough levelling was done to make ditches and a grade of one and one-half per cent, he can understand that there was no necessity of removing solid rock; if they came to a rock they simply went around it. That is why the road cost only $12,000 a mile. It surprised me just as it surprised my hon. friend; in fact, after my client came .to me, I hesitated more than a year before I would take his case. I did not believe it was possible to build that kind of road, but I went over the route myself, and was satisfied then that my client was right.
Bearing on this question of cost, we put in evidence two offers to build. One was an offer made by the firm of William McDonald and Sons to build the whole road complete, excepting rails, bridges and right-of-way, for $107,778. The other was an estimate made by Mr. Pinder himself-the figures are in his own writing-to build the road complete, excepting rails, bridges and right of way, for $107,509. Then there was another estimate from George McPhail, one of the most canny railway contractors in the Maritime provinces, who agreed to build the road, leaving out rails, bridges, and right of way, for something like $112,000. So that all these men-all practical men, who knew what they were talking about-said they could build this road for from $105,000 to $107,000, excepting rails, bridges and right of way. As a matter of fact, it turned out that the road was built for much less than that. Under the - evidence of Mr. Brown, the engineer, which I have read, William McDonald and Sons did all the grading on the first six miles, excepting that done by Claude McDonald, They put in all the concrete pipes and cedar culverts, laid the tracks, did the ballasting and everything to make the road complete on he first six miles for the magnificent sum of $24,109.10, or about $4,000 a mile. In addition to that Claude McDonald had done work on that six miles amounting to $6,400, which would add 
about another $1,500 a mile. According to these figures, all the grading, pipes, culverts, track-laying, ballast and everything of that kind for the first six miles would amount to about $5,500 a mile. McDonald and Son did all the grading on the. second six miles, excepting about one hundred feet, a fill just before the line comes to what is called the Naka-wick bridge. They did a portion of the track-laying and a portion of the ballasting; whatever it was, it amounted to $34,874. In other words, the McDonald estimates amounted to $58,983.17. It would take some time to read the evidence, and I will not attempt to do so, but McDonald swore-and my hon, friend will find his evidence on this point at pages 49 and 55 of the return which I have in my hand-that they could have completed this work-the grading, ballasting, and everything that was to be done-for $5,575. As I have said, Claude McDonald had done $6,400 worth; if you add these items together you get a total of $70,958 as the amount for which that road could have been built, in so far as the grading, ballasting, drainage and track-laying were concerned. In making up my estimate, I did not take the evidence of McDonald in full, because McDonald was claiming damages from Mr. Pinder on account of certain things he claimed he had done and had not been paid for. But McDonald had sued Pinder in the same court; they were simply quarrelling over a sum of $1,250.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
What has become of that
suit?

It has been settled; I understand that Pinder paid McDonald about $1,250 and costs. I am not positive, but I think that is about correct. In- the conduct of this suit, Mr. Pinder was required to file in the court the particulars of his set-off against McDonald. Mr. Pinder ad-mittted that he had paid McDonald only $58,000 or $59,000 in cash, according to the engineer's estimate, but he claimed that McDonald owed him a . certain amount in the way of damages and other things, and he brought his account against McDonald- money, goods, damages and ail-up to $68,000. In making up the estimate as to the cost of the road, I took $68,000 as the amount which the road cost, that is, McDonald's share of it, although I know that the figures are at least $8,000 more than they should be. I am satisfied that with what money Pinder has since paid McDonald, it will not exceed $60,000

although I have placed the figure at $68,000. But, as I said before, I think $60,000 would be the outside figure. McDonald's work was not finished when he left. There still remained most of the ballasting and tracklaying on the last six miles, and about three hundred feet of a fill to be made before they came to the bridges. Mr. Pinder would not give us any information whatever as To the cost of this. He had no books and no papers. I never saw as blank a wall in my life in any court house as Jim Pinder was. He was there an absolute blank. But he brought a witness, a Mr. Jackson, a foreman from the Canadian Pacific railway, who had done a certain amount of the work, and taking the total time of the men Jackson claimed he had under him-and again Jackson had no books or papers-but taking the total number of days possible we figured out $12,000, and therefore we added $12,000 to this as the amount done by Jackson to finish up the road. We came next to the bridges. I want to admit that I do not believe that the estimate which I have placed on the bridges is high enough. I was unable to get any evidence from Pinder, but I did have the evidence of the plaintiff, who said that Pinder told him the bridges weighed 56,000 pounds each, and that they bought them from the Canadian Pacific railway at somewhere about $20 a gross ton. So, figuring this up, and allowing for the cost of erection, we put them at $2,500 for the two. I may say that the only items we have not covered by actual evidence are the cost of bridges and the turntable and water tank.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Is that $20 a gross ton delivered on the road?

Yes, that is what
Stewart says Pinder told him and Pinder did not deny it. But I find I have not any other direct evidence as to the value of the bridges.
Is that 56,000 pounds each, or 112,000 pounds, supposed to represent the items of 358,000 pounds from the sale of bridges, two steel bridges, in this statement certified by Johnson?

Yes, that is the same
item. The evidence is that there were two bridges, one a pony truss and the other a through truss. The pony truss was 74 or 75 feet long and the other 103 or 104 feet long. I want to be perfectly fair about this, because I have so much leeway in this that I could add in all the cost that 93
Johnson put on and it would not affect the thing	a particle.	Not	long	ago,on a railway train coming from St. John to Montreal, I met an engineer of the Canadian Pacific railway, a gentleman	well known to	many	ofmy hon. friends opposite, who knew something about this suit. He introduced himself to me, told me who he was, and commenced talking about the suit as he had seen it in the newspapers, and he evidently knew what	the bridges	cost.	From	hisstatement I	am inclined	to think the	two
bridges cost from $5,000 to $6,000. I thought at the trial that the amount we assumed was light, and I was glad to get this information. Therefore I am satisfied that that amount should be increased.
We come next to the rails and fastenings, frogs, switches, etc. I had a great deal of difficulty in getting at that because, as my friend the Minister of Marine will understand, my client was not, a millionaire and we did not feel like bringing the Canadian Pacific railway down from Montreal to give evidence in that suit. However, after a good deal of working, we got from the Canadian Pacific railway a letter which was used in evidence, and I think it will satisfy the House as to the 9 p.m. cost of the rails, fastenings, switches, etc. This is an original letter, signed by Mr. A. Harshaw, who, at that time, was superintendent of the Woodstock Division:
Woodstock, N.B., January 5th, 1914.
F. B. Carvell, Esq.,
Woodstock, N. B.
Dear sir,-Further to my memo. January 3rd regarding prices of rails and fastenings sold J. K. Pinder of the Southampton Railway Company, prices quoted are merely those used by our Company as a standard appropriate value of stock on hand and do not represent the actual value of the material. X might also add that the Accountant came across the official order, D 4890, issued by our general agent, Mr. Bender, quoting a price to Mr. Pinder of $25 per gross ton. If you were passing Mr. Allan will show you this order.
Yours truly,
A. Harshaw.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Was that letter put in, in
evidence?

No, not exactly. That letter was submitted to counsel, Mr. Teed. Mr. Teed examined it and finally admitted it, which amounted to the same thing. I cannot say that the letter would appear on the records of the court, but the admission by the defendant's counsel would appear there.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I was curious to know how such a letter could be put in evidence.

Simply this: admit it or we will bring the Canadian Pacific railway officials here to prove it. My friend, Mr. Toed, who is .always very courteous, willingly consented, and .admitted the letter and the memo, attached to the letter. The memo, is as follows:
Mr. F. B. Carvell,
Woodstock, N.B.

Not $25 but $20, and, Mr. Speaker, you remember the evidence admitted .by Pinder afterwards was that this was the price delivered on tihe work. (Reading):
24,348 feet 52 pounds rails $20 per ton.
55,443 feet 52 pounds rails at $12 per ton.
Fastenings, 3098 jjairs 52 pounds flsh plates at 111 cents per pair.
220 pairs 52 pounds flsh plates at 6 cents per pair.
In addition to the above, the following material was supplied from this district.
