A. Harshaw.
Does that give the number of tons?

No, that gave the feet. I can tell my hon. friend that that amounted to about three-fifths of the whole, between three-fifths and three-fourths of the whole amount; and in making our figures we took the rest of them at 56 lbs. I do not know' whether the remainder were 56 lbs. or not, they were all second hand rails taken from branches of the Canadian Pacific railway, and, as you will see, considerably over one-half of them, nearly two-thirds of them, were 52 lb. rails, and we assumed anyway that the balance were 56, so at least it was stated. Figure that out and you will find that $28,000 would more than pay for the rails, fastening, frogs, switches and fish plates. The spikes had to be new, .and we had evidence that they would amount to about $1,700.
I come next to the right of way, because, as (I said, the right of way was in .addition to the .amount of these contracts. We had the evidence of Stewart that while he had the contract he made a contract with every owner of land along the right of way save five, and these averaged somewhere about $20 an acre.

We have the positive evidence of one man representing about two miles of road, and he put it at $2 or possibly $2.50 an acre. It was swampy land, with no timber on it, and practically useless. From the evidence which we were able to produce, $25 was the outside figure and we put it at that for the sake of the estimate. The road is only four rods wide, and there will be about 104 acres in the right of way. Roughly we put the right of way at $25 an acre.

That is supposed to
represent the $8,000 item?

Yes. The next is clearing. I am glad my hon. friend is following because his engineer estimated that it was worth $80 an acre to clear this land. The evidence of the men who did the work- there is no guesswork about this-shows that about 40 acres of land were cleared at $25 or $26 an acre-altogether only $1,000. So his officer is only $4,760 out on that little item. The next item is sleepers. The evidence shows that there were practicaliy no first-class sleepers. The majority were second-ciass, and from 10,000 to 15,000 would be nothing but culls. They were made from any wood growing in the country, a few of cedar, and the remainder of spruce, hemlock, fir or anything at all that would make a sleeper six inches thick with a five-inch face. We had evidence after evidence that these sleepers would not cost thirty cents apiece, and some did not cost more than fifteen cents. However, we figured them at thirty cents, and figured at a sleeper every two feet, or 2,640 to the mile, gave $10,000 for sleepers. The telephone line was $200 a mile. I know something about telephone lines. My company builds telephone lines for $100 a mile, $200 is away out. Fences were put down in the officer's estimate at $1 a rod. I must read a little evidence on this question of fences, which shows the character of the official who was doing this important work for the Department of Railways and Canals, or ft shows that the official was told to do something which he ought not to have done. I do not know which it may be, and I am not much concerned. Perhaps the plainest evidence of the culpability of this transaction is in regard tc the fencing. Practically the first witness I called was H. W. Maxwell. My friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries knows him very well.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not know him personally, but I know who he is.

He is a brother of
David Maxwell and has been in the engi-

neering and contracting business all his life. H. W. Maxwell was the superintendent of construction of the first six-mile section during 1911, and was a sub-contractor on the second six-mile section in 1912, and therefore had a pretty good knowledge of the road. He gave his evidence, and between that and the close of the trial I got him to go over the road again. He spent two days critically examining everything, taking notes, and came back and gave evidence. My friend will find this question of fences on page 92 of the report. I will just read it to him:
Q. Describe the fencing? A. Starting at the terminal we found fencing on William Cronk-hite, it was No. 9 7-strand wire, nailed on posts, I should think the wire would cost about 22 cents a rod delivered. The posts are cedar running from 3 inches to 6 inches at the end. They are as small as 3 inches at the top end. These posts were not closer together than 30 feet. I find where they crossed one man they were over 60 feet.
Q. Taking the character of the fencing as you saw it, what would you say it would cost to build it? A. Forty cents a rod.
He was examined on that very closely, but he stuck to his evidence. He said any man could go there and see for himself. Two months after Johnson made his report, he said there were not more than seven miles of fencing on the whole road, a distance of thirteen miles. The fencing which he saw was posts three inches in diameter at the top end, and sixty-three feet apart. How an officer of Johnson's standing could report this fencing to be all completed and to be worth a dollar a rod passes my comprehension, but there is the evidence and there are the facts. We come next to the culverts, that is the concrete pipe. The evidence is that there was 720 feet of that. We had the evidence of one man that he would deliver them on the right of way for one dollar a lineal foot. That was W. H. Maxwell, who had been in the concrete business for very many years. He said a dollar a foot would be a good price. In addition to that we had the evidence of Mr. Stewart who went over the road and measured every culvert:
After it was completed?
Yes. Stewart found that there were even less than 720 feet-some 670 feet or 680 feet-but I took the outside figures.
Did Brown swear to that statement?

No, the only thing
Brown swore to, was his estimate which I 934
have read that there was in the first contract 122 feet of pipe; in the second contract 598 feet, which added together gives 720 feet. As I said before, Mr. Stewart measured it and made about 680 feet. That was so near the amount in the estimate that I took the estimate. We come next to promotion and engineering. I could not get any evidence from anybody as to what the engineering cost. Pinder had no books, and would not tell us anything. Brown had no books, and did not know how much he had received or was going to receive. But we did ascertain the number of months and the number of men on the work. Brown was there about four or six months, practically most of the time. He visited the place once a month after that for a time. They had a couple of young men acting as resident engineers and rodmen. Figuring the matter out the best way we could, we ' came to the conclusion that $2,500 would be more than Pinder paid for engineering, and therefore it went down in the statement to that extent. In addition to that I have allowed $2,000 for promotion expenses, that is, preliminary work, surveying, etc. That gives for promotion and engineering, $4,500, which I am satisfied is away above the actual money paid. We have the evidence of a number of men, as to what the turntable cost. The company would not tell what it cost, but taking the evidence of Maxwell and George Pinder, we find that George Pinder gave the lumber in it at a ccst of $20 per thousand, which I think was a fair price for the kind of lumber used. You cannot figure out more than $1,500 as the cost of that turntable, though it appears in Mr. Johnston's report as costing $4,500. I tried to get the invoices and I could not. The turntable was bought from the Canadian Pacific railway; it was a second-hand table, fifty-five feet long, set upon a concrete centre, with a pit lined on the inside with cedars, cut with a bandsaw, so as to make, the arc of a circle. We had a number of witnesses examined as to the amount of lumber in this turntable, as to what it would cost, and all that, and we figured it at $1,500 as the outside limit of the cost.
I come to something now which is extremely interesting from Mr. Johnson's standpoint, and that is with reference to the station houses. Mr. Johnson was there in November, and Mr. Maxwell was there about the middle of January, so that Mr. Johnson was there about two months before Mr. Maxwell, and Mr. Johnson reported that the two station houses were worth

$5,000. I am going to read the evidence of Mr. Maxwell, as to the dimensions of these station houses, and hon. gentlemen can form an idea as to what Mr. Johnson's judgment- is worth on a question of this kind. At page 88 of the return, I read:
Q. What else did you see?
A. A station house.
Q. Describe the station house; you are speaking about the one at the terminal?
A. Yes, the station is 33 feet long, 16 feet 7 inches wide, 10 feet high and posts, finished in three apartments, a waiting room, a little office, and a freight room. The little office and the waiting room are sheathed overhead, and on the walls; the freight room is not sheathed, finished on the outside, clapboarded and painted.
Q. That is at the terminals?
A, Yes.
Q. What other station houses did you find?
A. That is all, I found at Mr. Pinder's, that is a little smaller than the other. This was 25 feet long, 15 feet wide, and 8 feet high. It is subdivided just the same into three compartments.
Q. Did you find any other station house?
A. No.
No wonder the Minister of Marine smiles at this description. Two little station houses, one thirty-three feet long, sixteen and a half feet wide, and ten feet high; the other twenty-five feet long, fifteen feet wide, eight feet high, set upon posts, built of ordinary rough lumber, shingled on the outside and painted, two-thirds sheathed on the inside, and the balance an open freight shed, and Mr. Johnson says they are worth $5,000 to build them.

No, $2,500 each. I am not a builder to any great extent, but I had very careful men go over the thing for me, and I was told that it was out of the question that they could possibly cost $500 each. One witness put them down as low as $350 each, but I will take them at $500 each or $1,000 for the two. I leave it to any gentleman in the House or out of it to figure it out, and if he can make them cost more than $500 each there must be something wrong with his figures. Next, we come to the engine house and the coal sheds. An officer of the department found that the engine house and the coal sheds would cost $2,500. Here again I will give the evidence of Mr. Maxwell as to their size, and the minister can figure out the cost himself:
I found an engine house, 81 feet long by 16 wide and 13 feet high. It was a pitched roof, shingled all over on the outside. I could not get in. By looking in the window I could only see a track and a walk on the side, not finished inside.
It was simply a shell, not finished on the inside, one thickness of boarding, ordinary 2x4 studs, and shingled on the outside, and Mr. Johnson says it cost $2,500.
Does that include the platform ?

There is no platform about it; I am speaking of the little shed where they run the engine in at night; I think it holds two engines. In addition to that there was a coal shed, and, while I do not know Mr. Johnson includes that in his cost, it was 30 feet long by 12 feet wide by 8 feet high, set rough, not shingled, boarded on the outside, set on posts.
These are all the buildings which were found on that whole railroad, excepting two platforms, each about 100 feet long and six feet wide. That is all there is to it with the exception of the water tarik. I was not able to get any information as to the bridges and the water tank, but what information I had as to the bridges I have given. Mr. Maxwell says that the water tank was the best building he saw in the whole lot. He says:
The water tank is 18-7 by 27 on the outside, and 20 feet high.
Q. So far as you could say, what would it be valued at?
A. It was clapboarded on the outside and planed. I could not see through the inside; it is a very nice building outside.
Q. How did this building compare with the others?
A. The very best of all, a very nice building.
We estimated the water tank at $1,000, which seemed to be the outside cost from the best evidence I could get.
Does that represent the $3,500 on this estimate ?
That is the $3,500 on this estimate. Then there are a lot of small items such as logs in cribs, $235, and lumber for building bridge floors.
There is an item of $1,750 for logs in cribs.

It ought to be about $225. Let me tell the minister that we had the man who actually counted the logs on the work, and he gave us the dimensions of the logs and the work done, and you could not make more than $225 out of that item.
I come next to the lumber and the bridge floors. Mr. Johnson estimated that at 28,000 feet at $50 a thousand or $1,400. There were only three or four pieces of hard

pine in the whole road; they got some old hard pine out of a bridge somewhere and used that as a sort of blocking under the coal shed, and these three or four pieces of old hard pine under the coal shed were the only pieces of hard pine on the whole road.
This is the bridge floors on the two iron bridges.
They are spruce.

He just says 'timber in
bridge floors.'

I know he does. He
puts them in at $50 a thousand. Those bridge floors are spruce. I will give the minister the dimensions of them. This is from the evidence of Mr. Maxwell:
Q. What kind of lumber was it? A. Spruce.
Q. What do you estimate the lumber in this, taking the cross ties at about 41 feet, every log a length of 70 feet, outside dimension? A. Yes.
Q. 100 would be 7,000 feet? A. Yes.
Q. Would 8,000 feet cover all the lumber in that bridge? A. Yes.
Mr. REID. That would mean 16,000 feet for the two.

Yes, or 15,000 feet.
Q. What did you find at Finder's mill? A. A bridge 82 feet long.
Q. What lumber was there in that? A. 78 ties in that one, 8 x 10.
Q. Stringers? A. 6 x 8.
Q. What kind of lumber? A. Spruce.
Q. These ties are larger than in the long bridge? A. Yes.
Q. How long are these ties? A. 13 feet.
Q. Did you figure this out? A. I have not yet. I get 78, 13 feet long, 8 x 10 x 80.
Q. That would be about 7,000 feet. A. That is all there is.
Q. Longitudinal 6x8? A. Yes.
Q. Would 8,000 feet cover the lumber in that bridge? A. It certainly would.
This is a man who measured every tie, every timber, every stringer, every longitudinal, every piece of wood in the road, and he says 15,000 to 16,000 feet will cover every stick of timber in the two bridges. Mr. Pinder, a member of the company and a son of Mr. James Pinder swore that $20 a thousand would be a fair price for that lumber. At that price you have $300 for the timber in those bridges, whereas an officer of this department puts it at $1,700.
Then, the stone in the culverts, $1,000; platforms, $100. In addition to that, Mr. Pinder swore that before the Canadian Pacific would take this road over in the fall of 1913, they compelled him to do some extra work in the way of trimming, putting on a little extra ballast, cleaning out the ditches and putting the road in a little
better condition. He estimates that work at about $300 a mile. I have extended that and called it $3,900. Then he says that they also required him to furnish some extra ties for rotten ones that had gone into disuse. He estimates that he simply left on the ground about 1,500 ties. I extend that at 30 cents a tie or $450. In addition to that, he had to pay the Canadian Pacific $700 to get them to take the work off his hands. I put that down. If there is anything in tha world that could come into the construction of that railroad that I have not put down, I would like to know it. I have the right of way, the fences, the telephone lines, the grading, the culverts, the track laying, the ballast, the rails, the bridges, the ties, the station houses, the turntables the water tanks, the platforms, everything that was mentioned by any and every witness in the whole trial which lasted for twelve days, everything that any engineer could tell me, and I have sworn evidence of every item excepting the bridges and the water-tanks. If you add all these up, you will find the amount is $157,618 as the absolute outside cost of that road. That is tin cost under unbusinesslike principles or methods, with the construction extended over two years, when it might have been done in one year, done in every way possible to m ke it more costly than it ought to have been. Mr. Pinder, or rather his counsel admitted for him that they got $155,000 of bonds from the province of New Brunswick guaranteed at four per cent.
At this point I wish to show where they got the last bond guarantee. The first bond guarantee was $10,000 a mile. The next bond guarantee was for $2,000 a mile. My hon. friend the member for York, New Brunswick, Mr. McLeod, was a member of the Government of New Brunswick at that time. I do not accuse my hon. friend of being a party to this nefarious transaction. We sometimes disagree very seriously, but we do not disagree on this point. How in the world my hon. friend the member for York, New Brunswick, or any other member of the legislature could have voted for the legislation giving this man $2,000 extra per mile is something that passes my comprehension, unless he believed this old man or unless he did it wdthout having engineers' certificates, without taking the most ordinary precautions known to the man in the street. They set forth in the preamble of their legisla-

tion, chapter 46 of the statutes of New Brunswick in 1913, as follows:
Whereas, owing to the exceptionally heavy rainfall of the past year, to the scarcity of labour and the consequent increase in the amount paid for wages, to the increased cost of railway ties, and other material, on account of the unusual amount of railway construction now being carried on in the province, to the generally expensive character of the work, and to the unfavourable conditions for disposing of bonds in the financial markets, the cost of construction of the Southampton railway has been very largely in excess of what was anticipated ; and whereas it is deemed expedient to further aid in the construction of the said railway-
And so on. They therefore gave him $2,000 a mile additional, or $26,000. This legislation was not passed until March 1913. In the course of the trial this matter came up. This road was built under contract. Mr. Binder himself did rot do a yard of grading. Mr. Pinder sublet all the grad; ing, all the ballasting and track-laying to other people. I have here the evidence of the people who did the work.
On page 51 of the return in the evidence of Robert McDonald, is the following:
Q. And the contract for the second six miles was entered into the same month?-A. Yes.
This was some time in March 1912.
Q. Which price you have given us?-A. Yes.
Q. Did you receive any extra price or greater amount of money by reason of the weather conditions during the next summer?-
That is the summer of 1912, when the legislation says that there was so much rain fall.
A. We received a large price on our common excavation, on our rock and on our gravel, and on the track-laying.
That is the contract for a larger price, but the contract was made in March before they knew what the conditions were to be.
Q. Was that on account of weather conditions or on account of the contract you made in March, 1912?-A. For the simple reason that we found there was not enough in for the first figures, the weather had nothing at all to do with it.
Q. You made a contract regardless of weather conditions? A. Yes.
Q. If there were bad weather conditions what would it mean to you? A. We would be the losers.
The contractor had completed the road for the schedule price made by him in 1912. And the legislature resolved that on *account of the weather conditions in 1912 it would cost more to build this road, and

so they made this man a present of $26,000. There are a couple of other items to which I wish to call attention, and then I am through with this branch of the subject. The acting Minister of Railways will note that in this report of Mr. Johnson 12,800 yards of solid rock is allowed for. The progress estimates only show, as I have already stated, a little over 4,200 yards; that is all there was in it, all that Mr. Ptinder paid for. Mr. Johnson's report also shows 5,500 yards of earth excavation under water at $2 a yard, a total of $11,000. My hon. friend will be surprised when I tell him that there was not one yard of earth excavation under water, and not a cent paid for such excavation. This item is a pure fabrication on the part of somebody. Another item was 24,000 yards of loose rock and hard pan at 70 cents, making a total of $16,800. And, as I have told the minister, there was not a yard of earth under water nor a yard of loose rock ot hard pan on the whole contract. Here you have $27,000 added to the cost of this road which is absolutely false, an absolute fraud by somebody-and it is that somebody I *am trying to get at, or trying to get the minister after him. Now, I could refer my hon. friend to page 34 of the report, where he will find the following:
Q. What were you to get for the grading? A. 30 i cents a yard.
Q. What were you to get for the rock? A. $1.25.
Q. For loose rock and hard pan? A. I have not got anything for that yet.
Q. Was there anything in the contract for that? A. No, there was not.
Q. What did you get for the grubbing? A. $75 an acre, on the first contract no clearing, the first was force account, earth 30J cents cub. yards, no loose rock or hard pan, the grubbing was $75 an acre.
Q. Earth excavation under water? A. We had no price on that.
Q. Did you get any pay for it? A. Have not yet.
Q. No price for earth excavation under water, you did not get $11,000? A. No, we did not.
Q. Did you get anything for overhaul? A. No, we have not seen it.
Q. Was there any contract for overhaul? A. None yet.
There are three items-excavation of *earth under water, loose rock and hard pan and overhaul, amounting to about $29,000, *and there is nothing in the specification or *in the contract about the removal of a yard of that material, yet the Department of Railways and Canals have included that in the cost of this work for the purpose Of paying a subsidy upon it. One can hardly conceive it possible that an engineer of

the department could make such a report unless he was told to do so by somebody.
I have tried to discuss this matter calmly, in an almost judicial manner-and perhaps some of my friends opposite .are surprised that I can discuss such ,a matter in a noncombative spirit as I have done this evening. Well, I do not intend to change my tone now. I say I cannot understand how an officer of any department could send such a report to his chief unless somebody told him to do so. Now, I am going to say something of which I have no proof; but I can get proof. I do not wonder that the acting Minister of Railways (Mr. Reid) looks at me. It will be remembered that there was an election in the county of York in December and January last. The sitting member is now Mr. Justice Crockett, and an election had to be held to fill his place. This Mt. Pindar was a member of the local legislature and a very prominent man in the county of York. He has been known for many years as the 'king of the Mackawick.' Now, this king of the Mackawick had one of two things in mind -either he must go into the New Brunswick government as successor to Mr. McLeod, or else he must come here to Ottawa to Tepresent the county. Things got pretty hot in the party caucus in the county of York. The newspapers stated about that time, and I have never seen it contradicted, that Mr. Pinder was told that if he would behave himself he would get a double subsidy for his road. Now, as I *say, I have no absolute proof-
Oh.

Let not the hon. member be too ready or I might be tempted to tell just what I do know about it. I will give it to my hon. friend privately if he wants it. The statement was made that I have just quoted and has not been denied. One fact is that Mr. Pinder had been trying to get this double subsidy and has failed. Another fact is that he got it in the month of November, 1913-$32,000 in hard cash that he was not entitled to and that he could not have got if this one monstrous report had not been made by Mr. Johnson. Mr. Pinder went to the convention and got up like a nice little man and' nominated my hon. friend from York (Mr. McLeod) as the most fit and proper person to represent the county in this House.
But it did not make any difference whether he did or not.
But he did it. And he got his $32,000. These are the facts. Of course, it is open to my hon. friend to explain them his own way.
They synchronized.

Yes, we have to thank the Minister of Finance (Mr. White) for that word; it seems to fit so many occasions. There is the synchronism, and at is up to hon. gentlemen opposite to explain it as best they can. As I have said, in order that this man should get this subsidy the road must have cost $21,400 a mile. I have shown that the road never cost more than $157,615 altogether. To make it perfectly plain, I am going a little further, because there might be something to add to or take from the total value of the securities and subsidies. Mr. Pinder got, as I have said, $155,000 four per cent New Brunswick bonds. I realize that there would be some discount in disposing of the bonds.
He says that it cost him something like $9,000 to dispose of the bonds. He swore to that, and we were so glad to get him to swear to anything that we accepted it, but with a wonderful degree of mental reservation. The first $50,000 of these bonds were paid to him in April, 1912, when 4 per cent New Brunswick bonds ought to have sold at pretty nearly par, and the second $50,000 were paid to him in October or November, 1912, when, again, New Brunswick 4 per cent bonds must have sold at about par. The last $55,000 were delivered to him some time in the autumn of 1913, and I am willing to admit that probably he had to sell them as low as 90, and that he would lose about $4,500 discount. Then, he said he paid interest. I could not accept the amount of money claimed for interest, because we have in the evidence of Mr. McDonald, the man who built the road for him, the fact that at no time had Pinder paid him more than $15,000 or $20,000 before he got his bonds. After he got his $50,000 bonds he could pay all his indebtedness and have $10,000 or $15,000 left to put in the bank. There is no doubt about that; we proved it absolutely. Then he went on with the second contract and got the second lot of bonds. After paying all his liabilities, according to the estimates he would still have $10,000 or 15,000 left to put in the bank. At the- same time he got $48,000 in subsidies from the Dominion Government, and after paying for the rails he must have had a tidy sum left. Under any circumstances, he got from the Government more

than enough money to finance the road, and there could not have been the amount of money paid out in interest which he claimed there was. He would not produce his bank books, they went so far as to subpoena the banker, but they were afraid to put him in the box, and so we were unable to hear his testimony. Pinder may have had outside transactions; in two or three years he may have paid out the interest he mentioned, but we could not figure up more than Si,500 interest, and therefore we put it down at that. Then he says he paid interest on bonds amounting to $8,100. That, I believe, is correct. Add these together and you have 818,100. The cash received from the Government was $81,280, face value of bonds $155,000, a total of $236,280. Subtracting from that the discounts, interests, etc., $18,700, you have $217,580 net cash which this man received from the Government of Canada for a road which could not have cost him more than $157,615. I know this figure is thousands of dollars above what it actually cost him, but taking the figures which I have here to-night, a profit of $59,965 is left to Mr. Pinder.
I think I have submitted to this House tonight a state of affairs which calls for action of some kind. I think the acting Minister of Railways will agree with me in this. I am not making any charges now; I am not here for that purpose. I am not saying what became of the money, because I do not know. I do not believe that Pinder was allowed to put all that mon^ into his own pocket.' I know the men with whom he was dealing, and I want to tell the House that Mr. Pinder was just as good as some of the other men with whom he was dealing. I do not believe that the men who are running affairs in the province of New Brunswick to-day will allow Pinder to put $60,000 of this money into his own pocket, having passed legislation such as I have described, giving him these bonuses, first $10,000 a mile and then $2,000 a mile after the road was completed. Then there was at first the single subsidy from this Parliament, and later a double subsidy. It does not seem to be possible, but if it is, then I can only say that the King of the Mackawick is a much more wily politician than I gave him credit for, because he or somebody has pocketed $60,000 of good Government money for building a little tramway line less than 13 miles in length. I ask the acting Minister of Railways what he is going to do about it.'5 If he doubts

my evidence, I may tell him that I have produced nothing to-night that was not sworn to in open court in the presence of a judge and jury. I want to assure him that Mr. Pinder did not lack for counsel, because he had three of the best counsel in the province of New Brunswick, and everything was done which human ingenuity could devise in order to pull him out of this scrape. Not one solitary effort was made to prove that this road did cost more than I have estimated, excepting, perhaps, the evidence of Mr. Johnson, the Canadian Pacific railway man. With that exception, not a book, not a paper, not a plan, profile, invoice or letter was produced to show that this road cost more than we claimed it did. They simply said: we will give you no information about it; we will rest on the strength of the allegation that this contract was obtained by fraud, and if we cannot win upon that we cannot win at all. The jury disagreed. One of the questions of fact left to the jury was: was the contract obtained by fraudulent representations made by the complainant to the defendant company? Four of the jurymen said yes, and the others no. The result was a disagreement; a verdict was found for the plaintiff on a number of collateral items amounting to $162. The main question stands for trial later, and in all probability as soon as we get through the session of Parliament, we will have to get at it again and have it settled. But that was a matter between Mr. Stewart and the railway company; it now becomes a matter for the Minister of Railways, and I would like to know what he is going to do about it. I must have proved to him to-night, by the sworn testimony which I have produced, that a great wrong has been done. I do not say by whom; I do not say by the Minister, or by Mr. Johnson, although I do say he was the agent, but I do know that a great wrong has been done. As a matter of fact I am not sure that Parliament would not have been justified in paying him a single subsidy, because the statute reads as follows:
The Governor in Council may grant a subsidy of $3,200 per mile for the construction of each of the undermentioned lines of railway which have cost more on the average than $15,000 for the mileage subsidized.
Strictly speaking, therefore, the minister might have paid a single subsidy of $3,200 a mile for the road, even if it did cost an amount slightly less than $15,000 a mile-although it is always supposed that a road must cost that amount before such a subsidy may be paid. But the

moment you reach $15,000 a mile and the moment you pay $3,200, you have to have $1,000 of cost for every $500 of subsidy. If you divide the cost which I have estimated, $157,615, by 13 miles, you have about $12,100 a mile. This man got bonds and subsidies to the extent of $18,400 a mile on a road which cost him about $12,100 a mile -got it on the false and fraudulent reports of an officer of the Department of Railways and Canals. Something like $38,000 or $40,000 was absolutely abstracted from the revenues of this country, fraudulently and on false representations.
I would like to know what the minister will do about it. I think that not only should there be a Parliamentary investigation., tout that a Royal Commission should be appointed. This is a scandal so great that we ought to know the whole of it, we ought to know who is really at the bottom of this crime, because a crime it is. We ought to know whether E. V. Johnson is the sole culprit or whether he has wily associates. We ought to be in a position to investigate this thing to the very bottom. We ought to know who profited from the $40,000 taken from the coffers of this country unlawfully, illegally. I think that the minister is recreant to his duty, and, in the presence of the Prime Minister and of the Minister of Marine, I say that I think the whole Government is recreant to their duty if they do not appoint a Royal Commission and have this matter investigated, to find out who is the culprit and bring an action against Pinder and the railway company for the restoration of at least $40,000 of this money, wrongfully taken from the people of this country by these false reports. I know by the report of Mr. Johnson that he was accompanied on his second trip by Pinder. I do not know whether he saw Brown or not but I believe he did. I cannot account for Brown's remarkable action on any other hypothesis than that he accompanied him.
Mr. Brown was with him on one trip.

That was in the year
before.

Yes.
Mr! CARVELL: I have set out before the House the facts; I have brougnt in nothing except sworn evidence. I have shown that over $40,000 was illegally taken away from the people of this country, and I call on the Minister of Railways to take whatever steps may be necessary in order to rectify
the wrong which has been done and to place his department in such a position that there will be no repetition of such dishonest transactions as I have described to you here to-night.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. REID (Acting Minister of Railways) :
speechtext:
I wish to say at the outset that there is no objection whatever to bringing down the papers asked by the hon. member for Carleton, N.B., (Mr. Oarvell). I was glad to hear that the hon. member had no fault to find with the road. Neither had he any fault to fiud with the Government for granting a subsidy. The whole fault that he has to find in connection with this matter is because the subsidy has been paid on an amount that he claims was not earned. I am very glad indeed that this matter has been brought forward: If the statements made by the hon. member for Carleton are correct, then certainly Mr. Johnson has not done his duty as an inspector for the Railways and Canals Department. I would say that I listened to the hon. member throughout and I thought he put his case in a very fair and reasonable way, with one exception; that was that, he threw out an insinuation that in some way Mr. Johnson had done a wrong and that he had been urged in some way to commit this wrong. Now there is only ohe man that he could refer to and that would be the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Cochrane). Let me say that I take issue with the hon. member at once, and say that as far as the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals is concerned I believe that from the time the subsidy was voted up to the present time he knew nothing other than what the officers of his department certified to. I have before me the papers in connection with this matter. When I saw this notice on the Order Paper, I asked Mr. Johnson what there was in 10 p.m. connection with it so that I would be able to give any information required and to discuss it in a proper manner if the hon. member should make any remarks in connection with this order. Mr. Johnson stated to me, as has been proved by the certificates read by the hon. member, that he went over this road himself on two different occasions, that he gave it a very careful inspection ; and the statement as read by the hon. member for Carelton in regard to these items that go to make up the cost, Mr. Johnson assured me, in the office of the Minister of Railways and Canals, that he had gone over very carefully and that he

was quite satisfied that every one of them was correct and true. He gave me the following memorandum:
Ottawa, February 16, 1914. Memorandum re Southampton Railway
Company.
In reference to the estimate of cost of Southampton railway, the undersigned begs to submit that he obtained the quantities from Mr. Brown the engineer of the road, and, from an examination of profile and after two inspections of the road, is satisfied that estimate fairly represents the amount of work done and that the prices are fair and reasonable. Mr. Brown's first estimate, before the work commenced, was $242,508.60 or $18,654.50 per mile. As the work progressed it was found that the quantities and in some cases the prices had been underestimated and in October, 1912, the undersigned submitted an estimate amounting to $288,617, or $22,726 per mile. On completion of the work, when it became practicable to ascertain the actual cost, the latter was slightly increased, showing a cost of $22,954 per mile.
Respectfully submitted,
11. V. Johnson,
Inspecting Engineer.
This certificate shows that Mr. Johnson went over the road twice, and he states himself that he went into the matter very carefully. The hon. member has submitted a statement as I mentioned a few minutes ago showing the different quantities and cost in connection with this railway, and he makes several statements that are amazing to me. For instance, he has made the statement that of the earth excavation under water, 5,500 yards, certified to by Mr. Johnson, not one particle was done.
That is right.

I am very much surprised
to hear a statement like that. He also says that of solid rock excavation there were only 4,200 yards, while Mr. Johnson certifies to 12,800 yards. He also certifies to the right of way. Where Mr. Johnson has put it down at $8,000, the hon. member puts it at about $2,500 or less. My hon. friend also tells the House here this evening that the two steel bridges that Mr. Johnson estimates at a cost of $17,900 cost only some $5,000 or something like that. I did not take down the exact amount.

I omitted one item. The minister will find that abutments are put down at $7,400. I have sent out my extracts to ' Hansard,' but I think that was the amount. Cunningham swore that he got $3,101 for building the abutments.

All along the line, the hon. member has stated that Mr. Johnson's estimates were far in excess of the actual cost.
I do not know the exact rules which guide 
the inspector when he is inspecting railway work to see whether the subsidies may properly be paid. This is the first occasion since I have been looking after the Railway Department in the absence of the minister that I have had to discuss subsidies to railways. When I knew this matter was coming up I made inquiries of the chief engineer of the Department of Railways, Mr. Bowden. He has been there for six or seven years, and so far as I know, the Minister of Railways and Canals has the greatest confidence in him. The minister's predecessor, the hon. member for South Renfrew, also had the greatest confidence in Mr. Bowden, I understand. It was not only on Mr. Johnson's report that the minister acted. Mr. Johnson made his report to Mr. Bowden, his superior officer, and it was Mr. Bowden's duty to go into that report. On November 5, I find that Mr. Bowden made a report in connection with this matter as follows:
L. K. Jones, Esq., I.S.O.,
Assistant Deputy Minister and Secretary, Department of Railways and Canals, Ottawa, Ont.
Sir,-I have the honour to report on the result of an inspection made on October 23, 1913, of the Southampton railway.
Under the Subsidy Act of 1912, chapter 48, section 2, item 23, the right to grant subsidy to the Southampton railway was given, [DOT] for a line of railway from a point at or near Millville to a point on the St. John river near the Pokiok bridge: not exceeding 13 miles.'
A subsidy agreement was entered into on May 14, 1912, and a supplemental subsidy agreement on October 26, 1912. The actual length of the line is 12.7 miles and the inspection shows the line completed throughout in accordance with the requirements of the subsidy agreement. The estimated total cost of road is $291,517 or $22,954 per mile.
I wish to draw' the attention of the hon. member for Carleton, N.B., to the clause which follows:
I certify that the line is completed in accordance with the requirements of the subsidy contract and that the company is entitled to payment of full subsidy of $6,400 per mile on 12.7 miles or a total of $81,280, less previous payments.
I am, Sir,
Your ohedien servant.
W. A. Bowden,
Chief Engineer.

I was coming to that.
Mr. Bowden's report is based on Mr. Johnson's report.

Of course, Mr. Bowden knew nothing of this matter other than what Mr. Johnson's report told him, but unless Mr. MARCH 9, 1914
Bowden had confidence in Mr. Johnson, an official under him, I am satisfied he would never have signed such a report. On looking up Mr. Johnson's record I find that his position is that of inspecting engineer. He first entered the service of the Intercolonial railway on May 3, 1869 as a subordinate on surveys. That shows that he must have had experience in railway building. From that time he has done nothing but railroad work. He joined the Canadian Pacific engineering staff as assistant leveller in May, 1871. At that time the Canadian Pacific railway was being constructed under Government supervision by the Public Works Department. Mr. Johnson was transferred to that department in connection with the Canadian Pacific railway-draughting office in 1872 and remained with the Public Works Department until the Department of Railways and Canals was set apart in 1879. He was appointed assistant engineer of railways on January 1, 1900, and was appointed inspecting engineer on January 1, 1902. That is his record. He is an old official and I feel that having been so long in the department it would hardly be fair for me to censure him as he would deserve if the statements of the hon. member for Carleton, N.B., were correct. I feel that 1 should be allowed to take up to-morrow with Mr. Bowden and Mr. Johnson, the whole matter as it appears in 'Hansard,' and I shall certainly demand from them an explanation. Perhaps they may be able to give me some light on this matter that will put an entirely different construction *on it. I certainly' hope so. I should be very sorry to think that Mr. Johnson after having been so many years in the service would certify to that statement, if it were *of the kind described by my hon. friend. I hope the hon. member for Carleton will withdraw the insinuation that the Minister of Railways knew anything other than that this w-as a fair and straight matter. The hon. member knows that the subsidy' granted by this Government, even the double subsidy of $6,400 per mile, was very much less than the railroad would cost, even at his own figures. Unless the minister knew about the guarantees having been given by the New Brunswick Government, he would feel justified in paying the amount, realizing that the cost would exceed much more than the subsidy called for.

So far as the Minister of Railway's is concerned, 1 do not think for a moment that Mr. Cochrane had anything to do with it, but the department
would know they could only pay the double subsidy if the road cost $21,400 per mile, regardless of where the money to build it came from.
I admit that, but the minister .is responsible for the submission of the Order in Council bo pay the subsidy.

Theoretically, I admit
that.

The only information the
minister has as to that is what the chief engineer gives him. Mr. Bowden sends his memo, to the minister certifying that such a road has earned the subsidy, and on receipt of that memo, the minister makes out a certificate for the subsidy. That is all the minister knows about the matter, and that is all the Minister of Railways or this Government knew about this. I am glad the hon. member has brought this matter before the House. I shall take it up to-morrow with the officers of the department, and I shall go into it very thoroughly.
I trust this discussion will do good in the future, in reference to the inspection of lines for subsidies. I shall be only too pleased to bring down the return at the earliest possible moment.

I did not intend to take part in this discussion and the part I shall take will be very briefly done. I take it, from the very moderate way in which my, hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Carvell) has placed this question before the House- and sometimes he is not very moderate- and from the language he has used, that he is not making any attack upon the Government. I have no brief for this' railway, and my hon. friend knows it. The hon. gentleman has said that Mr. Pinder received this subsidy ' in order that he might be good.' It was a matter of no importance to me-and I live in the same constituency with him and was his colleague in the provincial legislature for six or seven years-whether Mr. Pinder was good or not. It was a matter of no importance to me whether Mr. Pinder stood up in the convention and nominated me or not. The facts are that after he had received this isubsidy he came to me in my office and said he would like to nominate me, and I said: Very good, Mr. Pinder, I shall be very glad if you do so. There are hundreds of men in the county of York, carrying as much weight, whom I would have been much more pleased to have had nominated me, and whose nom-

ination would have been equally effective. So far as I know, and I think I do know, there was absolutely no arrangement whatever, except in the mind of my hon. friend, and no connection whatever between the nomination of myself by Mr. Pinder and the receipt of this additional subsidy.
I think I ought to say to the House that I am familiar, very familiar, with the facts laid before this House by my hon. friend (Mr. Carvell). I ought to say also, that I fully concur in many of the statements he has made. He has not been able to bring it home to the Government-I do not think he has attempted to do so-that any wrong has been done, or has been attempted to be done by the Government. I do not think my hon. friend attempts even to insinuate that Mr. Johnson, the engineer, has been guilty of deliberate wrong. But I say, and I think I ought to say, that Mr. Johnson, the engineer in this case, when he made such a report as he did make, made it having been deceived as to the actual facts of the case. I believe that that report is not, in all its details, a correct statement of the cost of the specific items that went into the construction of that road. I 'have kept pretty well in touch with, and I have been familiar with the construction of that road since its inception, and I say, from my own knowledge gleaned by living on the spot and by talking to the men whom my hon. friend has cited to-niglyt as having given evidence in the case of Stewart vs. Southampton Railway Company, I am in a position to know that many of these items are padded items, and these items whi h Mr. Johnson has accepted, and upon which, very properly, the Department of Railways, accepting his statement, paid the subsidy, are not true and correct .'statements jot fact in regard to what went into the construction of that railway.
I am not here to attack anybody, but in order that the House may know Mr. Pinder's attitude to-day, Mr. Pinder is held up as a wily Tory politician. Mr. Pinder has been for many years a member of the Conservative party, but I had occasion during this Session to go home to my constituency to take a hand in a contest in which a young man was nominated to fill the seat in the local legislature which I resigned to come to Ottawa. That young man was nominated at a regularly called convention of the Conservative party, and I had occasion to go home to fight for that young man, not against the Liberal party but

against a gentleman and a very reputable gentleman whom this same man Pinder was backing with all the power he had. Now, Mr. Pinder nominated me, and for many years he had a fictitious reputation for great strength in the constituency I represent, but we had a showdown on this occasion and we beat Mr. Pinder's candidate by 644 votes, notwithstanding that we had the Liberal party against us, and all that Mr. Pinder covld do, in addition to that.
No, not the Liberal party.

I think I know it better than my hon. friend does; I think I know the county of York better than he will ever know it. My hon. friend came into the county of York once, in a by-election some time ago, and he discovered that we beat his candidate then by 1,200 votes, although the hon. member spent some time in the county. I know the county of York; I have been over it every inch, and there are not many men in it that I do not call by their front names. However, Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to enter upon a discussion; I merely desired to place myself on record as agreeing with many of the facts presented here to-night, and I believe that the Acting Minister of Railways will investigate this, and thoroughly investigate it, and if a wrong has been done he will do his best to set it right. But might I suggest that when he starts to get any money back from James K. Pinder, he is up against a real hard proposition.
My hon. friend .suggested a moment ago that there was $57,000 that did not go into this railway; that somebody had it in his pocket, and that he did not believe that James K. Pinder had it all in his pocket.
I do not know where the money has gone; but if Mr. Pinder ever got it, he has got it yet. I am going to be very fair to-night.
I do not believe that Mr. Pinder has got much of this money. Mr. Pinder is not a good business man. My hon. friend will admit that. Mr. Pinder built that road in a slipshod way. He did not take advantage of the conditions to build that road in the most economical way. I know that. I do not know whether Mr. Pinder has any money or not, but my hon. friend will not dare to charge against any man in New Brunswick or in Canada that he has received one dollar of that money wrongfully

from Mr. Pinder. If he could, he would, but he cannot. Nobody received any of that money wrongfully, and not one dollar of it went to any campaign fund. My hon. friend will not charge that it did.
I have said these few words frankly and fairly, not wishing to take part in this debate but simply wishing to place myself, as representative of the county of York, New Brunswick, in a proper position in regard to the matter, so that my constituents may take notice of the fact that I do not countenance anything of a public nature that I know to be wrong.

I think I have been in
Parliament long enough to know that it is not my province nor my place to make charges against any man unless I have the proof behind them, and I have been pretty careful in that regard. I have very strong suspicions of a good many things about that $60,000. I have very strong suspicions as to how this report was made to Mr. Johnson and by Mr. Johnson to the Government. I have very strong suspicions as to why the report was made as it was, and I have stronger suspicions as to why the last $3,200 was paid to Mr. Pinder. All these suspicions and all the statements and challenges made by my hon. friend from York, New Brunswick only emphasize the statement that I made .some time ago to the Minister of Railways that, if ever a statement had been presented to this House which demanded not merely a departmental investigation but an investigation by a royal commission, my statement to-night backed up by my non. friend the member for York, New Brunswick, was one. It is not in my motion and I cannot incorporate it in my motion; but, in the remarkable and frank corroboration of my statement by the hon. member for York, New Brunswick, in not only the insinuation, hut the statement that in his judgment Mr. Johnson is not the real sinner in this case, I think the case is doubly strong. Therefore I hope not only that the Minister of Railways will conduct a departmental investigation, but will%ppoint a royal commission and have this matter sifted to the very bottom.
Motion agreed to.

That, in the opinion of this House, it is expedient to provide that no person, by himself, his agent or otherwise, shall manufacture, sell
or give away any cigarettes, cigarette papers or wrappers, or any substitute therefor, or shall be in any way concerned in such manufacture, sale or distribution, or authorize or permit the same; that no cigarettes, cigarette papers or wrappers shall be imported into Canada or entered for consumption therein, and that all cigarettes, cigarette papers or wrappers intended as such shall be subject to seizure by any officer of Customs or Inland Revenue, and that they, with the packages in which they are contained, shall be disposed of under regulations made by the Governor in Council; that penalties shall be imposed for the contravention of this Act, and the prosecution for any such penalty or punishment may be brought and prosecuted under the provisions of part xv of the Criminal Code relating to summary conviction.
He said:	The subject matter of this
resolution has had the attention of a good many people and of a good many countries for the last few years. It may be considered by some to be a very drastic proposal; but the reasons for its stringent provisions, to my mind, arise from the fact that nearly all the provinces have had laws proposing to deal in part with this question, and so far they have been very ineffective. It is difficult to say for what reason the provincial laws limiting the use of cigarettes by youths up to different ages, in some provinces 16, in some 15, in some as high as 18, have been ineffective, but the evil effects of cigarette smoking by young boys or youths under twenty are very well known throughout this country.
There is no principle so dear to the Britisher as that of personal liberty, but the question has come to this, whether on the part of the strong there should not be some sacrifice in the interest of the weak. I am quite aware that a good many reasonably fair minded men cannot go as far in their judgment as this resolution proposes to go.
We know that if one thing should be considered more carefully than another not only in this House but by every right thinking citizen it is the careful guarding of our citizenship. In view of the injury that is so apparently done throughout the whole country by the use of cigarettes, it is a question bow far this question of cigarette smoking should be curtailed by the goodwill and common sense of the people.
I do not wish to deal at great length with the question as to whether cigarettes hurt the young or the old, or this class or that; but I wish first to point out the appalling increase in the use of cigarettes in Canada and in other countries as well. Go into the United States and you will find that fifty years ago, so far as any records that can be found are concerned, the first

Does the mover of this resolution include pipe smoking in his resolution? From a word or two which he dropped during the course of his remarks, I fancy that he does. He says it is hard for the mother to chasten the children when the father sits in the corner smoking -not necessarily cigarettes. Whilst, of course, everybody agrees that the excessive use of cigarettes, like the excessive use of anything, may result in grave injury, I do not know that we are prepared to go as far as the words ' or any substitute therefor ' in the fourth line of the resolution. I have looked up the various authorities on the subject, and I find that the word ' substitute ' in this case certainly does not mean that what is used in the place and stead of the cigarette shall be in the form of a cigarette. It may be a pipe, and if these words refer to the pipe, then this is a very-serious resolution. I do not think the people of this country are prepared to abolish the pipe. In speaking about it to the hon. gentleman himself, I asked him, as I did not wish to take him by surprise, what he thought about it. Well, he said, if it means that, let it all go. He does not smoke himself, so he does not care, but I say that a great many people in this country are not injured by smoking; they enjoy their pipe, and would be greatly injured if they did not have it. Whilst it is a well-known fact that no athletic trainer will continue to train any one who smokes cigarettes, because of their effect upon the heart,

the same thing does not follow with regard to the pipe. Of course, the trouble in all these things is to find a point at which to stop. You will observe, Mr. Speaker, that the Ten Commandments have gone by the board. The hon. gentleman does not refer to them; he does not think that the ten or even the eleven commandments are sufficient. For myself, I am inclined to think that the eleven commandments are enough. Whilst the Chinese and the Japanese, who have somewhat similar methods of enforcing their ideas, may proceed to administer five or six thousand blows with a bamboo for every infraction of an edict, are we to say that the whole principle of moral suasion should be abandoned in Canada because the moral ground in which the good seed is sown is so sterile that it is no longer fit and proper soil for the cultivation of good principles? Are we to have no other recourse but to put offenders in prison, hammer them, punish them or confine them? Is it no longer possible to show them the evil of their ways and to beseech them to be men, that they may exert that self-control which alone makes a man? or are they simply going about as trees walking, are they to be clothed in the garments of men, but not clothed and in their right minds. We are going to work up in this country, unfortunately, it seems to me, a lot of weak-kneed individuals, people who must be led around by the ear, or else they will not do what is right. I have the utmost contempt for the silly boy or girl who must be fed with a spoon or out of a bottle until probably he or she is twenty-one years of age. That kind of rot ought to be done away with, and if it is necessary to re-introduce the methods of our friend King Solomon, we will introduce them. But it cannot be said that all of the good women who are urging on the hon. gentleman who is the mover of this resolution, have exercised, in the matter of dress, an example of the self-control which we should have wished for; and I have no hesitation in saying that if they would reform themselves in that particular they would do as much good as ever they will do by asking us to give up our pipe and tobacco. These things can be carried too far. Mind you, I must not be construed as speaking in favour of the cigarette. I am well aware that it has done immense damage, and that possibly it may have to be repressed just as opium smoking in China has had to be repressed. At the same time we must not think that the panacea is to be found in universal repress-
ion; we must exercise some common seaise and some self-control if we are to evolve into the highest type of manhood.

upon a person's chances in life. It saps the vitality necessary to success. I make that statement without any reservation. It blunts the sensibilities and deadens the thinking faculties. There are thousands of cases in which we know that to be true. It kills ambition and the finer instincts and the more delicate aspirations and perceptions, because it destroys the ability to concentrate the mind which is the secret of all achivement. The mover of this resolution pointed out the deteriorating effect of tobacco on the rising generation. If we want to make the people of this country strong, sturdy, and intelligent we must discourage by some means the use of the cigarette. I know of no habit that will decrease a boy's mental and physical forces so much as the cigarette. Magistrate Oraine of New York city made the following statement a short time ago:
Ninety-nine out of a hundred boys between the ages of ten and seventeen years who come before me charged with crime have their fingers disfigured by yellow cigarette stains.
. .	. I am not a crank on this subject,-
Note that. He is not a crank. He has scores of cases before him of boys charged with various crimes. He goes on:
I do not care to pose as a reformer, but it is my opinion that cigarettes will do more than liquor to ruin boys. When you have arraigned before you boys; hopelessly deaf through the excessive use of cigarettes, hoys who have stolen their sisters' earnings, boys who absolutely refuse to work, who do nothing but gamble and steal, you can not help seeing that there is some direct cause, and a great deal of this boyhood crime is, in my mind, easy to trace to the deadly cigarette. There is something in the poison of the cigarette that seems to get into the system of the boy and to destroy all moral fibre.
A case came to my notice a short time ago in which a boy in New York had robbed his mother and actually beaten her because she would not give him money to buy cigarettes. As further evidence of the deadly effect of the cigarette, I may cite the experiment of a chemist. Not long ago he took the tobacco used in an average cigarette and soaked it in several teaspoonfuls of water and injected a portion of it under the skin of a cat. The cat almost immediately went into convulsions, and died in fifteen minutes. Dogs have been killed with a single drop of nicotine.
Dr. J. J. Kellogg says:
A few months ago I had all the nicotine removed from a cigarette, making a solution out of it. I injected half the quantity into a frog, with the effect that the frog died almost instantly. The rest was administered to another frog with like effect. Both frogs
[Mr. Thornton.!
were well grown, and of average size. The conclusion is evident that a single cigarette contains poison enough to kill two frogs. A boy who smokes cigarettes, twenty cigarettes a day, has inhaled enough poison to kill forty frogs. Why does the poison not kill the boy? It does kill him. If not immediately, he will die sooner or later of weak heart, Bright's disease, or some other malady which scientific physicians eveywhere now recognize as a natural result of chronic nicotine poisoning.
There is no doubt that cigarette smoking has killed thousands of boys, and sooner or later it will injure seriously every boy who indulges in the habit. The bon. gentleman who moved the resolution, gave very plainly the reason why grown men are not affected, and it is that they have become mature, while the boy is immature. The boy will soon find that the cigarette is bad for his 'heart, as the doctors all tell

Another distinguished magistrate whose name I will not mention, says:
Yesterday I had before me thirty-five boy prisoners. Thirty-three of them were confirmed cigarette smokers. Today, from a reliable source, I have made the gruesome discovery that two of the largest cigarette manufacturers soak their product in a weak solution of opium. The fact that out of thirty-five prisoners, thirty-three smoked cigarettes might seem to indicate some direct connection between cigarettes and crime. And when it is announced on authority that most cigarettes are doped with opium, this connection is not hard to understand. Opium is like whisky, it creates an increasing appetite that grows with what it feeds upon. A growing boy who lets tobacco and opium get a hold upon his senses is never long in coming under the domination of whisky too. Tobacco is the boys' easiest and most direct road to whisky. When opium is added, the young man's chance of resisting the combined forces and escaping, physical, mental, and moral harm is slim, indeed.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I take the ground with the mover of the resolution, and I take it very strongly, that if we want a sturdy and vigorous manhood in this country we have to do something to suppress this vice of cigarette smoking, which is sapping the energy of the boys and young men of this country. I do not know of any more effective way of calling the attention of the country to the injury that faces them in this direction, than the move my bon. friend from Dundas (Mr. Broder) has made to-night. I have the greatest pleasure in heartily endorsing what he has said.

Before the motion is put, I would like to say a few words. The subject which the hon. member for Dundas (Mr. Broder) has brought to the attention of the House this evening, is one that has been discussed

The evil which does undoubtedly exist, through the excessive use of cigarettes, particularly by those of immature years, has been placed before this House, in very cogent terms, on different occasions. The theory upon which hon. gentlemen chiefly relied in former years, was, that cigarettes, particularly imported cigarettes, were supposed to be impregnated or adulterated with drugs, and also, that persons who used cigarettes were in the habit of inhaling the smoke and in that way causing serious injury to the system. Another theory has been introduced tonight, which I have not heard before: that some peculiar combination of the paper and tobacco results in the creation of a byproduct which is very poisonous. Apart from these circumstances, I have not been able to see very clearly why it is that the smoking of tobacco when rolled up in a litle piece of paper is more harmful than if smoked in the form of a cigar or placed in a pipe. I have no douibt that there is a great deal in the theory that the detriment through inhaling is very great, and it may be, although I have no knowledge of the subject except what I have heard stated in tne House, that cigarettes imported from abroad do contain other deleterious elements than tobacco, such as noxious and harmful drugs. Representations have been made in this House, and they have been made to the Government from time to time since we assumed office, as to the very great evils which result to the youthful portion of the population of Canada from cigarette smoking. It is alleged, not only that it is very detrimental to the physical condition of young persons, but that it also does have a marked effect upon their mental and even their moral condition, through the deterioration of their physical condition.
I have taken the liberty sometimes of saying to those who have made these representations before me, that I am quite sure that paternal influence would be, or at least ought to be, of more value than all the legislation we could pass here, so far as young persons are concerned; and that if paternal and family influence were to-day of the same force which they exercised twenty-five, or thirty, or forty years ago, perhaps we would hear less now of the need of such legislation. I cannot say that anything that has been said in reply to that, suggestion from me has altered my opinion very much in that regard. It does seem to me that, at the present day, we are getting 94j
more and more into the tendency of having family discipline placed under the guidance of direct legislation, instead of under the exercise of paternal influence, which in the case of a great many members of this House would have stamped out the cigarette evil at a very early age, if it had made itself manifest. You may place all the legislation you like on the statute books of Canada, and you can never quite replace the force and effect of parental and family influence, whether in regard to the use of cigarettes or in regard to the use of anything else.
This subject was discussed twice in Parliament before-first in 1903 and then in
1907,	and the late Administration placed upon the statute book of this country, in
1908,	legislation about as restrictive as any one could desire, that is, short of an attempt to prohibit absolutely the importation, manufacture, and sale of cigarettes. The legislation was introduced by Mr. Aylesworth in the session of 1908, in the form of a resolution prohibiting any person under the age of sixteen years from purchasing cigarettes; and it also dealt with minors who should undertake to smoke or chew tobacco on the public street so as to create an offence in the view of persons passing by. The Committee of the Whole House to whom the Bill was referred increased the age limit to eighteen, but it was reduced to sixteen by the Senate. The Senate also made some minor changes of another character in the Bill. The Bill, however, as passed was fairly drastic. It declared that:
Every one is guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction in the case of a fust offence to a penalty not exceeding ten dollars, and in the case of a second offence to a penalty not exceeding twenty-five dollars, and in the case of a third or subsequent offence to a penalty not exceeding one hundred dollars, who, directly or indirectly, sells or gives or furnishes to a person under the age of sixteen years any cigarette or cigarette papers, whether for his own use or not, or sells or gives or furnishes to such a person tobacco he knows or has reason to believe is for the use of that person.
There was an absolute prohibition of the sale of cigarettes to any person under the age of sixteen; not only that, but a prohibition of the sale of cigarette paper to any such person, and finally a prohibition of the sale of tobacco to any such person in all cases whether there was reason to believe it was for his use or for the use of some one else.
The second section of the statute to which I allude provides that:

It shall be the duty of any constable or person having the powers of a constable, or person authorized so to do by any by-law in that behalf made by any authority or person having power to make such by-law to seize any cigarettes, cigaarette papers or tobacco in any form other than cigarettes in the possession of any person apparently under the age of sixteen years whom he finds smoking or chewing or about to smoke or chew' tobacco in any street *or public place.
Just what the test should be with regard to a person who might be found about to smoke or to chew on the street, I do not know; but thr statute is in that form.
Then there was a penalty for juvenile smoking. The section is very long, and I will not weary the House with it, but the prohibition is very strict and the penalty severe. The chapter to which I allude is chapter 73 of the Act of 1908, and the section to which I have reference is the third section of that statute. In the fourth section there was a provision whereby, if an automatic machine for the sale of cigarettes or tobacco was found to be used by persons under the age of sixteen, authority was given to punish that offence and if necessary to confiscate the machine itself and all the tobacco and cigarettes in connection with it; and so on through many sections of the statute. It is a pretty strict statute on the whole and one which, if enforced, would largely prevent any great evil or detriment resulting throughout this country from the use of cigarettes or tobacco by persons under the age of sixteen years.
I have inquired of my hon. friend from Dundas (Mr. Broder), and of delegations who have pressed this subject upon the attention of the Government, as to why it is that any further legislation is required when there is already legislation on the statute book which, if enforced, would to a great extent do away with this evil. The only answer that I have received up to the present time, either from my hon. friend the member for Dundas or from any person who has come before me, is that the statute is not enforced. If a statute such as this, which is plain in its terms and which ought to be easily capable of enforcement, because it relates to matters carried on before the eyes of every person in the community, is incapable of enforcement for some reason or another, possibly for the reason that it is not properly supported by public opinion, I would like to know for what reason we should expect that a statute prohibiting the importation manufacture or sale of cigarettes would be enforced more effectively than the present

statute. We have a boundary line to the south of four or five thousand miles; and I do not know hoiw many miles of sea-coast on both the east and the west; and if there is that desire on the part of Canadians, both young and old, to use cigarette's, which would seem to be manifest from the non-enforcement of this statute, and if public opinion is so lax -that .a statute of this character cannot he and is not enforced, I would like to understand for what reason and upon what principle anyone would expect that a statute isuch as my hon. friend from Dundas proposes would be any more effectively enforced. In respect .to matters of this kind you cannot depend upon putting words upon the statute book. Well, you say to me, we propose to do something more than place words upon the statute book; we propose to enact a law prohibiting the importation, manufacture and sale of cigarettes, and we propose to enforce it. How do you propose to enforce it? How many thousand men would lit he necessary to have upon our southern boundary, upon all our sea-coasts, in every oommiunity, town, village and hamlet in this country, in order to enforce a law of that kind? Would it not be infinitely better to have upon the statute book of this country some moderate law capable of enforcement and really enforced, than to put upon the statute book a most extreme .and drastic measure of this kind and never attempt to enforce it at all, and, more than that, never be able to .enforce it at .all. That is the way the matter strikes me at the moment; and up to the present time, neither in this House nor outside of it, from delegations or otherwise, have I been able to hear reasons which I would regard as sufficient against those which I have placed in very brief form before the House.
However, the subject .to which my hon. friend has called attention is undoubtedly important, df it be true, as is alleged, that the use of cigarettes amongst very young persons, both boys and girls, is continually increasing, .and it may be necessary for legislation of some kind to be placed upon the 'Statute book. It may be necessary for us to place upon the statute book some provision which will assist in the enforcement of the present law which it seems to me is capable of redressing the evil in very great measure if properly enforced. I pass by for the moment the suggestion made by my (hon. friend from West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) that the mere fact that cigarettes or tobacco may

be used to excess by some persons, or by persons of immature age, is not necessarily a reason why we should prohibit its importation or manufacture.
I venture to say that any person who is curious in such matters could go into medical works and bring to this House very good evidence indeed that thousands of persons in Canada to-day are suffering physically and mentally from the excessive use of tea and coffee; and yet I do not think it would be suggested that we should absolutely prohibit the importation into Canada of tea and coffee.
I am willing that this resolution shall have the fullest possible consideration by this House or by a committee, and if there is any means by which the evil that undoubtedly does exist-if the representations made to me are true-can be mitigated, then any legislation for the purpose of redressing that evil should be placed upon the statute book. But I should hope and desire, so far as I am concerned, that that legislation will be reasonable in its character and capable of enforcement. For I think that no law at all in regard to such a matter as this is infinitelv better than an extreme law placed upon tlie statute book without hope or expectation of reasonable enforcement. A moderate law', a reasonable law, that can be enforced and made effective in a reasonable degree in redressing the evil, is to my mind infinitely better than a law not enforced at all, and not supported by public opinion. I am perfectly willing that the proposal of the hon. member for Dundas shall be submitted to a committee of this House with full power to inquire into the matter. The subject could be submitted to the committee in one of two ways. The motion the hon. gentleman has suggested could be passed pro forma, the House reserving its judgment upon any Bill introduced thereon until after further inquiry; or, better still, the resolution might be amended to call for the appointment of a committee that, I hope, would go into this question in a serious way with a view to improving existing legislation. So, I would suggest to my hon. friend that the resolution he has proposed might be amended; and I would move that it be amended in this way^
That all the words after the word 'that' in the first line of the proposed resolution down to and including; the word 'provide' in the second line of the resolution be struck out and the following substituted therefor.
A committee of fifteen members be appointed to inquire and report whether it is expedient to enact as follows;
That no person, by himself, his agent or otherwise, shall manufacture, sell or give away any cigarettes, cigarette papers or wrappers, or any substitute therefor, or shall be in any way concerned in such manufacture, sale or distribution, or authorize or permit the same; that no cigarettes, cigarette papers or wrappers shall be imported into Canada or entered for consumption therein, and that all cigarettes, cigarette papers or wrappers intended as such shall be subject to seizure by any officer of Customs or Inland Revenue, and that they, with the packages in which they are contained, shall be disposed of under regulations made by the Governor in Council; that penalties shall be imposed for the contravention of this Act, and the prosecution for any penalty or punishment may be brought and prosecuted under the provisions of Part XV of the Criminal Code relating to summary conviction.'
And by adding to the proposed resolution
at the end thereof, the following words:
Or whether it is expedient to make any other amendment and if so what amendment to the existing laws for the purpose of remedying or preventing any evils arising from the use of cigarettes.
That the committee have power to send for persons, papers and records to examine witnesses on oath or affirmation and to report from time to time.
Would it not be well to cover the ground of finding out why the present law is not enforced?
