speechtext:
I think that is quite
covered by the words, ' to inquire and report, whether it is expedient to make any other amendment and if so, what amendment to the existing laws?' I think that is sufficiently comprehensive to authorize the committee to enter upon the inquiry that the hon. gentleman suggests.

I
feel very diffident about supporting any proposal that would tend to restrict the liberty of the individual. At the same time, all law is a restriction of personal liberty and the only question is whether the law operates for the benefit of the individual and the community or not. We already have the liberty of the individual restricted with regard to the consumption of intoxicating liquors; we have it restricted with regard to harmful drugs; we have it restricted with regard to much more trivial matters as anybody can learn, if the next time he rides in one of the Ottawa street cars he reads the signs and warnings displayed for the information of the public, based upon a city by-law passed, it is to be presumed, in accordance with the wisdom [DOT] of the electors and councillors of this fair city. So, the proposal of my hon. friend from Dundas (Mr. Broder) is not objectionable because it is a restriction of individual

liberty. Our support or opposition to the measure must rest on some other ground than that. Evidence has been placed before the House to-night as to the harmful effect of the consumption of cigarettes and the growth of that consumption, and it is for each member to make up his mind as to whether the harm to the individual and the community is sufficiently great to warrant that measure of interference with personal liberty that would follow the passing of the resolution of my hon. friend or that might result from the amendment proposed. In regard to the reason why my hon. friend has proposed his resolution while there is legislation upon the statute book bearing upon the same question, I may take the liberty of suggesting to the House a possible reason for the course that he has taken. Under the legislation that is on the statute book to-day the enforcement of the law is difficult, because each attempt at enforcement may very well become the subject of proceedings in court. There might be a demand that evidence should be brought forward in support of any attempt to enforce the law. But under the provision that my hon. friend suggests, the evidence would be automatic; there would be no question of fact to interfere with the operation of the law. So that, provided public opinion was favourable to the enforcement of the very comprehensive proposal of my hon. friend, the terms in which it is worded would remove the difficulty that lies in the way of the law which is now on the statute book. The existence of the offensive article would be all the evidence necessary, and the difficulty of enforcement would be done away with. Under the present Act there are difficulties as to questions of fact; under the proposal of the hon. member for Dundas there would be no difficulties as to the question of fact, and it is, I presume, with this idea in view that my hon. friend has made his proposal. Of course his proposal is very comprehensive and goes much further than the statute. It is a matter for consideration whether the evil is sufficiently great to warrant that the law should be carried so far as the hon. gentleman proposes to carry it. For my own part, as I do not happen to use tobacco in any form, I would feel more delicate about advocating a course that would interfere with the right of any other man than if I were advocating a course interfering with action on my own part. To argue the question as a matter of right, however, it appears to me that it has been established that the cigar-
ette is an individual and national evil, and to my mind a sufficient case has been made out to warrant this House in adopting the resolution of the hon. member for Dundas as he represented it to the House.

Without going into the merits of the question raised in the resolution or in the amendment, there has been brought up an issue, to my mind, of much greater importance, to which I referred for a moment when I addressed the House this afternoon. It is this: What provision have we foj the enforcement of federal law? We have in this country a peculiar arrangement by which the enforcement of federal law, especially in criminal matters or in matters of this	kind,	is relegated
to the provinces.	If we are to pass
effective legislation, we must find a way to enforce federal legislation by federal machinery. In the United States they have a federal system similar to ours, and in all their legislation-take for instance the pure food legislation which has proved to be so beneficial-it is expressly stated that its enforcement shall be in the hands of the Attorney General of the United States. We have a very pleasant trick in this House of passing legislation for the improvement of society, but of making no provision for its enforcement, relegating that to the Attorneys General of the various provinces. We have been evading a grave responsibility which is placed upon this House. If we pass legislation of various kinds we must put in those laws provisions for their enforcement. We have to-day a statute creating a railway commission in Canada.

As I understand it, the original motion was based on the idea of providing an effective enforcement of the law.
